steps.text:
Checked, and the honest answer is **no — there's no linter rule that catches this**, and it's worth understanding why.

- **eslint-plugin-astro doesn't have it.** The closest rule, [`astro/missing-client-only-directive-value`](https://ota-meshi.github.io/eslint-plugin-astro/rules/missing-client-only-directive-value/), only checks that a directive *that's already present* has its framework value (`client:only="react"`, not bare `client:only`). It does nothing for a *missing* directive on an interactive component. The search confirmed there's no rule for "uses `useState`/`onClick` but not hydrated."

- **Why it's genuinely hard:** the interactivity lives in the component definition (`.tsx`) while the directive lives at the usage site (`.astro`) — different files. Catching it needs cross-file *and* framework-semantic analysis ("this imported component is interactive" ∧ "this usage lacks a directive"). Linters overwhelmingly work within a single file, so this falls through.

- **And we're on Biome anyway.** Even eslint-plugin-astro's partial coverage isn't available to us — Biome's `.astro` support is JS-parts-only and wouldn't do this cross-file reasoning. Adding ESLint just for this wouldn't help, since the rule doesn't exist there either.

There's a related plugin, [`@naverpay/eslint-plugin-use-client`](https://github.com/NaverPayDev/eslint-plugin-use-client), that detects interactive React features (hooks, handlers, browser APIs) to enforce `'use client'` — but that's for **Next.js RSC**, a different mechanism; it flags the interactivity, not the missing Astro directive.

**One partial safety net exists by accident:** a component that touches *browser globals* (`window`, `document`, `IntersectionObserver`) will usually **error at build** when SSR'd without `client:only` (`window is not defined`). So those get caught. The silent case is the pure `useState`/`onClick` component — renders to valid HTML, no error, just dead.

**In practice** people catch it by testing the interaction (the button doesn't work → you notice) and by discipline: *interactive ⇒ island*. Which is a decent argument for our plan — keep the poster deliberately **static** (no interactivity to forget), and make the genuinely-interactive surface (the control panel) an explicit island. The footgun only bites when interactive-and-you-forgot; a small, clearly-islanded interactive surface keeps that risk contained.

exchanges.prompt: Okay, that kind of sucks. I'm wondering if we can catch it at build time, to tell Astro to error if it strips out a useEffect or something?

steps.text:
Right idea, but here's the hard constraint: **Astro can't error on this natively, and it's not really "stripping" anything.** When Astro SSRs a React component with no directive, it's plain React server rendering — and effects *never* run during any React SSR (that's by design, even for `client:load`, whose SSR pass also skips effects). At the component's render moment, "no directive" is **indistinguishable** from "`client:load`, SSR pass" — the difference is only whether Astro emits hydration JS *afterward*. So there's no build-time signal "an effect was discarded" to hook into, and the component can't self-detect it either (with no directive, no client JS runs at all to notice it's dead).

So the only real path is **static analysis** — essentially building the missing rule ourselves. Two routes, and one is surprisingly cheap:

**Cheap & Biome-native (catches the hooks case):** A component that uses `useState`/`useEffect`/`useRef` *must* be an island — a static component has no business calling hooks (they won't run). So we enforce: **React hooks are only importable inside an islands directory.** Via Biome `overrides` + `noRestrictedImports` (`importNames` for `useState` etc.), any hook import outside `src/islands/` is a lint error in `ci`. That flips the footgun from "silent dead button" to "you used a hook in a non-island file — move it to islands/ (and hydrate it) or drop the hook." Runs in our existing `bun run lint`.

- **The gap:** a component that's interactive via a bare `onClick` but *no* hooks has no import to ban, so Biome misses it. Those are rarer (interactivity usually implies state), but not zero.

**Robust & custom (catches everything):** a small build/CI script that parses each `.astro` file and errors if an island-directory component is used without a `client:*` directive. Astro's compiler (`@astrojs/compiler`) gives an AST, so it's tractable — just more code than the Biome override.

**My recommendation:** we have *zero* islands right now, so building this is premature. Adopt the **convention now** — interactive components live in `src/islands/` — so it's a habit by the time it matters. Then when we create the first real island (the control panel), I wire the Biome hook-import ban (cheap, high-value) and, if you want belt-and-suspenders for the `onClick`-only gap, the `.astro` usage check too.

That keeps the poster static (no footgun at all there), and makes "interactive ⇒ island" a *lint-enforced* rule rather than discipline — just deferred until there's actually an island to protect. Want me to note the `src/islands/` convention in the plan and move on to the poster scaffold, or set up the Biome enforcement now even though it has nothing to guard yet?

steps.text:
The landscape is clear enough to narrow, but one thing decides it for us. Here's where things stand in 2026:

- **Runtime CSS-in-JS is out** — styled-components is in maintenance mode (declining), Emotion carries runtime + hydration cost. Not for new SSR projects.
- **Zero-runtime is the modern answer**, three real options: **vanilla-extract**, **Panda CSS**, **StyleX**.

But your **same-file** requirement + Astro prunes two of them:
- **vanilla-extract** — styles live in *separate* `.css.ts` files (same directory, not same file). Fails "same file." Out.
- **StyleX** — same-file and excellent (Meta's), but its **Astro** integration is undocumented/uncertain. Risky for our `.astro`-heavy setup. Out (for now).
- **Panda CSS** — same-file `css({...})`, zero-runtime, scoped atomic output, type-safe design tokens, and a **dedicated `@pandacss/astro` integration**. Fits every requirement.

So realistically it's **Panda CSS vs Tailwind**. The crux for us is that our poster is **SVG-heavy**, and there Panda's `css({ fill: '#2f6b3f', fontSize: 13 })` (real CSS properties) beats Tailwind's arbitrary-value utilities (`fill-[#2f6b3f] text-[13px]`). Let me verify Panda actually works cleanly *in `.astro` files* (not just React), plus its codegen/reset story — that's the one thing that would make or break it here:

exchanges.prompt: Oh, interesting. If astro's .month is scoped, then I think it's viable? Is there anything that tailwind / panda would give us that native astro doesn't?

steps.text:
Right — Astro adds a `data-astro-cid-*` attribute to both the element and the selector, so `.month` compiles to something like `.month[data-astro-cid-galvtxlt]`. It genuinely can't clobber another component's `.month`. So native scoped `<style>` is viable, and for the poster it's honestly great: colocated, scoped, **real CSS** (ideal for SVG), zero runtime, zero added tooling, and it handles `@media print` for the paper stuff.

**What Tailwind/Panda give that native Astro `<style>` doesn't:**

1. **They reach React islands (`.tsx`).** This is the real gap. Astro's scoped `<style>` only works in `.astro` files — a React component can't use it. So in our mixed project, native `<style>` styles the poster fine but *can't* style the control-panel island; you'd need a second mechanism there (inline styles / CSS Modules / css-in-js). Tailwind classes and Panda's `css()` work uniformly in both.
2. **A type-safe, shared design-token system.** Tailwind's theme / Panda's tokens give you autocompleted, type-checked colors, spacing, and type scale across every component. Native Astro gives per-component CSS; cross-component tokens you'd hand-roll.
3. Utility ergonomics (Tailwind) / `css()` composition + recipes (Panda) — preference, not a capability gap.

**But #2 mostly closes for free.** A single global stylesheet with CSS custom properties —
```css
:root { --peak: #2f6b3f; --available: #9ec9a4; --axis: #555; }
```
— gives you shared tokens usable *everywhere*: in `.astro` `<style>`, in React inline styles, in CSS Modules, all via `var(--peak)`. Not type-checked, but genuinely shared across `.astro` and `.tsx`. Put the reset in that same global file, imported once from a base layout.

So the honest picture for **our** project: it's poster-dominant (SVG in `.astro`) with a *small* interactive surface (the control panel). That tilts toward **native Astro `<style>` + one global CSS file (reset + tokens)** — zero new dependencies, and it covers ~everything. The only things you give up: type-safe tokens, and the React island bits get styled with a slightly different mechanism (inline or a CSS Module referencing the same `var()` tokens).

My recommendation: **go native + a global reset/tokens file now.** It's the minimal-tooling choice consistent with how we've built everything else, and the "reach for Tailwind/Panda" trigger is clear — *if the React styling surface grows or you want type-safe tokens.* We're not locked in; adding Panda later is additive.

Want me to set that up — a `src/styles/global.css` (reset + a first pass of design tokens), a base layout that imports it, and move the poster's inline hex colors to `var()` tokens? Then we keep the poster's structural CSS in its scoped `<style>`.

exchanges.prompt: How does astro .month work with React components? The styling has to be returned within the component JSX?
Okay, explain Panda as opposed to tailwind. I'm not familiar with Panda.

steps.text:
Sure. The one-line mental model:

- **Tailwind** = **utility classes** you compose in the markup — a naming DSL (`p-4 text-sm fill-gray-500`) you learn.
- **Panda** = **typed style objects** written with *real CSS property names* — `css({ padding: 4, fontSize: 'sm', fill: 'gray.500' })` — that a build step compiles into atomic CSS.

Both end up as **atomic, zero-runtime CSS** at build. The difference is the *authoring model*: Tailwind's utility strings vs Panda's CSS-property objects.

Here's our actual poster month label in each (plus native Astro for reference):

```astro
<!-- Native Astro: scoped <style>, .astro only -->
<text class="month">Jan</text>
<style>.month { fill: #555; font-size: 13px; }</style>
```
```tsx
// Tailwind: utility classes; precise values need bracket escapes
<text className="fill-[#555] text-[13px]">Jan</text>

// Panda: real CSS properties as a typed object
<text className={css({ fill: '#555', fontSize: '13px' })}>Jan</text>
```

**Key differences:**

| | Tailwind | Panda |
|---|---|---|
| You write | utility class names (`p-4`) | CSS properties (`padding: 4`) |
| Learning | memorize the utility DSL | you already know CSS property names |
| Type safety | string-based; needs an editor plugin, typos silent | TS-native — properties *and* token values autocomplete and type-check |
| Precise/arbitrary values | bracket escape: `text-[13px] fill-[#2f6b3f]` | just the value: `fontSize: '13px', fill: '#2f6b3f'` |
| Tokens | theme config (`@theme` in v4) | `panda.config.ts` tokens, generated as typed accessors |
| Variants | compose utilities / add `cva` | built-in **recipes** (typed component variants) |
| Setup | a Vite plugin + a CSS file | a Vite plugin **+ a codegen step** that generates a `styled-system/` dir (gitignored) |

**Where they land for us:**

- **SVG-heavy poster**: Panda wins on readability — `css({ fill, fontSize, stroke })` is just CSS, whereas Tailwind on SVG is mostly bracket-escaped arbitrary values (`fill-[#…] text-[13px] stroke-[1.5]`), which is where the "utility soup" gets ugly.
- **Type safety**: Panda fits the project's ethos (zod, strict TS, Biome) — invalid property or off-palette token is a *compile error*, with autocomplete. Tailwind is strings.
- **Setup cost**: Tailwind is lighter — no codegen. Panda adds a `panda codegen` step and a generated `styled-system/` directory (you import `css` from it), which is a real bit of machinery for a small project.
- **Both** work uniformly in `.astro` and `.tsx` (Panda's `css()` returns a className string), so both erase the native-Astro `.astro`/`.tsx` asymmetry.

So the trade is basically: **Tailwind = simpler setup, utility DSL, string-based; Panda = more setup (codegen), but real-CSS authoring + full type safety + cleaner SVG.** Given our SVG focus and type-safety leanings, Panda is the more *aligned* choice — but it's genuinely more machinery than native-Astro-plus-a-global-tokens-file, which remains the lightest option if you don't need uniform React styling yet.

If it helps you decide, I can show what our `Poster` would concretely look like in each (native scoped `<style>` vs Panda `css()`) so you can compare the real thing rather than a one-liner.

exchanges.prompt: Okay. Stepping back a little, well, quite a lot, I want to revisit the choice of astro. steps.text:
That's a fair reconsideration — Astro compatibility has been a recurring tax, and this is fundamentally a small static site. Let me first correct one thing in the framing, then research the real answer.

**Framing:** GitHub Pages serves *static files only* — it doesn't run a server, so `Bun.serve` never runs there. The question isn't "deploy Bun.serve to Pages"; it's "can **`bun build`** produce static files (HTML/JS/CSS) that Pages can host?" — and a GitHub Action builds them in CI, then publishes `dist/`. `Bun.serve`'s routing is a *dev-time* convenience, separate from the deployable output.

So the real questions are: does Bun's bundler produce a deployable static React site, does it give us *pre-rendered* HTML (which matters for the printable poster) or just a client-rendered SPA, and how's multi-page. Let me research the current state:

steps.name: WebSearch
steps.detail: Bun static site generation SSG React prerender vs SPA 2026 Bun.build HTML

steps.text:
Researched. Direct answer first, then a nuance that actually matters for your goal.

**Yes — Bun can build a deployable static React site.** `bun build ./index.html --outdir dist` scans the HTML for `<script>`/`<link>`, bundles everything, and emits static files ([Bun's HTML/static docs](https://bun.com/docs/bundler/html-static)). Multiple HTML files = multi-page (index + about); a client router handles in-app routes. A GitHub Action runs `bun install && bun build` and publishes `dist/` to Pages. So the deploy story is solid.

**SSG vs SPA — and does it matter for us?** `bun build` gives a **client-rendered SPA** by default (HTML shell + JS bundle; React renders in the browser). It does *not* pre-render HTML — that's what Astro gave us free. But for the **printable poster**, SPA is genuinely fine: you print *from a loaded browser tab*, where JS has already run and rendered the poster into the DOM. Pre-rendered HTML (SSG) only wins for no-JS/SEO/first-paint — nice-to-haves here, not requirements. And if we ever want it, DIY SSG with Bun is small (render the poster with `renderToStaticMarkup` in a build script; there's even a [`bun-ssg` template](https://github.com/pcmaffey/bun-ssg)). So SSG is **not a blocker** for dropping Astro.

**The nuance that matters for *your* stated goal.** You want to stop paying the compatibility tax. Dropping Astro removes the `.astro`-specific friction (Biome's experimental `.astro`, CSS-in-JS-in-Astro, the islands footgun) — real wins. **But the replacement bundler is the catch:**

- **Bun's own bundler** (`bun build`): all-Bun, fewest layers, simplest. *But it's the newer, less-trodden path* — most tools (Panda's PostCSS integration, CSS processing, plugins) document **Vite/webpack**, not Bun's bundler. You'd likely trade "does X work with Astro?" for "does X work with **Bun's bundler**?" — e.g., Panda + Bun-bundler is exactly the kind of thing we'd have to verify. So it doesn't necessarily end the compat-checking; it just moves it to a less-mature target.
- **Vite + React** (drop Astro, *keep* Vite): mature bundler, **universal ecosystem support** — Panda, Tailwind, everything "just works with Vite" because everyone targets it. This is the most-compatible way to escape Astro. Bun stays as your runtime + package manager + test runner; Vite is only the bundler/dev-server. Vite's `base` config + GH Pages is a well-worn path.

So, honestly: if the driver is "fewer compat surprises," **Vite + React is probably the sweet spot** — it removes the Astro layer *and* keeps the battle-tested, universally-supported bundler. Bun's bundler is the more radical simplification but the riskier one for exactly the reason you're frustrated.

**Migration cost is low right now** — we'd keep Bun, Biome, zod, the data model, the geometry, and the tests; only the framework/render layer changes (`Poster.astro` → `Poster.tsx`, `index.astro` → `index.html` + a React entry). Good moment to switch if we're going to.

My question back: given the goal is escaping compat friction, do you want **Vite + React** (mature bundler, safest escape) or the **all-Bun `bun build`** (simplest, but you'd be validating Bun-bundler compat for things like Panda)? Or, now that the `.astro` costs are itemized, does keeping Astro still look worth it?

exchanges.prompt: Vite would still run the bun runtime, right? We just wouldn't be using the bun builder? I'm okay with going to Vite then. We would still use bun test, and not vitest?

steps.text:
Two good clarifications — let me untangle them, because there's a subtlety in the first.

**On "Vite runs on the Bun runtime":** not quite, and this is worth getting right. Bun's roles stay: **package manager** (`bun install`), **test runner** (`bun test`), and **script launcher** (`bun run …`). But **Vite itself is a Node tool** — its dev server and bundler are designed to run on Node, and that's the compatible path (which is *the whole reason* we're picking Vite over `bun build`). So Vite runs on Node under the hood; you *can* force it onto Bun's runtime (`bun --bun run dev`), but there's no reason to and it's the less-tested path.

And to correct the framing: **we were never using "the Bun builder."** Astro bundles with Vite (rolldown-vite) internally. So the bundler is Vite in both the before and after — dropping Astro just removes the `.astro` layer *on top of* Vite. Net division of labor:

| Job | Tool |
|---|---|
| Package manager | Bun |
| Test runner | Bun (`bun test`) |
| Script launcher | Bun (`bun run`) |
| Dev server + bundler | **Vite** (runs on Node) |
| Typecheck | `tsc` (replaces `astro check`) |

**On `bun test` vs Vitest:** yes, keep `bun test` — no reason to switch. Our tests are pure logic (schema, geometry); they don't need Vite's transform pipeline, and `bun test` already respects the `@/` tsconfig path (verified earlier). Vitest only earns its keep if you're testing **React components that depend on Vite's transforms/CSS handling** (it shares Vite's config and has jsdom built in). We're not, so `bun test` stays; we'd only revisit if component-rendering tests get heavy.

A few migration notes so you know the shape (not doing them yet):
- Vite doesn't read tsconfig `paths` on its own — we add the small `vite-tsconfig-paths` plugin so `@/` resolves (Astro did this automatically).
- `check` becomes `tsc --noEmit` instead of `astro check` — which means **we can drop the TypeScript `^6` pin** (that existed *only* because `@astrojs/check` needed it) and move to TS 7 if we want. Nice side benefit.
- Biome's `.astro` override goes away — it's all `.tsx` now, which Biome lints fully (no experimental gaps, no `noUnusedImports` workaround).
- We keep everything else: Bun, Biome, zod, the data model, `lib/`, and the tests.

Want me to lay out the full migration as a concrete step list (what changes, what gets removed/added) before we execute?

exchanges.prompt: If we don't use vite and use bun build, how risky is that? Can we sanity check one or two of the riskiest compatibilties?

steps.text: Smart — let's not take my word for it. `bun build` is the newer path, so let me actually stress the riskiest bits in a throwaway project: **(1) does a React SPA bundle into a working static site**, and **(2) how does it handle CSS** — CSS Modules (scoping) and plain CSS. Those are the foundations everything else sits on.

React + plain CSS bundle cleanly (0.97MB JS is just React, fine). But one flag: the CSS Module output shows `.title` **unscoped** — bun may have treated `App.module.css` as plain global CSS rather than scoping it. That matters, since scoping-without-clobbering is your explicit requirement. Let me confirm CSS Modules and test the other big risk — PostCSS (which Tailwind/Panda need):

Correcting myself — the follow-up shows I misread the first result:

**`bun build` sanity-check results:**

| Capability | Result |
|---|---|
| React SPA → static site | ✅ builds, HTML rewritten to hashed bundles, deployable |
| Plain CSS | ✅ bundled |
| **CSS Modules** | ✅ **scoped** — `.title` → `.title_cmaZow`, present in *both* the CSS and the JS (mapped correctly) |
| **PostCSS** | ❌ **ignored** — a nonexistent PostCSS plugin caused *no* error; bun doesn't run `postcss.config.js` |

So the risk is **lower than I feared on the fundamentals**: React and — importantly — **scoped CSS Modules both work**. That already satisfies your hard requirement (scoped, no clobbering). The one real gap is **PostCSS**, which is exactly what **Tailwind and Panda** hook into. With `bun build` they'd need their *standalone CLIs* run as a separate pre-build step (generate CSS → bun bundles it) — workable, but manual, and off the documented happy path.

(One caveat the probe also surfaced: bun's *runtime* — `bun test`, `bun run` — doesn't map CSS Modules (`styles.title` was `undefined`), only the *bundler* does. Irrelevant for our logic tests, but it'd bite if we ever wrote component-render tests that import `.module.css`.)

**So the bundler choice now cleanly reduces to the styling choice:**

- **CSS Modules** (sibling `.module.css`, scoped, no clobbering; shared tokens via global CSS custom properties; no type-safe tokens) → **`bun build` is fully sufficient.** All-Bun, simplest, no Vite. Your scoped/no-clobber requirement is met; the only concession vs Panda is *sibling-file* rather than same-file, and untyped tokens.
- **Tailwind / Panda** (same-file `css()` or utilities, type-safe tokens) → **Vite** is the smooth path (first-class support); with `bun build` you'd bolt on their CLIs.

That's the real fork now, and it's a genuinely good result for your all-Bun instinct: if **CSS Modules** is acceptable styling — and it does meet your stated must-haves — then `bun build` is viable and the simplest stack, no Vite layer at all. If you specifically want Panda's same-file typed `css()`, that's the thing that justifies keeping Vite.

Which matters more to you: **maximal simplicity (bun build + CSS Modules)**, or **same-file typed styling (Vite + Panda)**?

steps.text:
Confirmed empirically — **I was wrong.** Tailwind v4 works with `bun build`: the build succeeded and the utilities actually generated real CSS (`.text-red-500`, `.p-4`, `.font-bold` all in the output). My PostCSS test was valid but irrelevant — Tailwind v4 uses a plugin, not generic PostCSS, so that test proved nothing about Tailwind. Apologies for the over-extrapolation.

**Corrected, empirically-verified picture of `bun build`:**

| | Result |
|---|---|
| React SPA → static site | ✅ native |

So the all-Bun path is more viable than I claimed. Two honest nuances remain, though:
- **`bun-plugin-tailwind` is community-maintained** (v0.1.2, ~9 months stale, some reported selective-styling bugs), *not* official. Bun's own docs are drifting toward recommending the Tailwind CLI "until there's a native plugin." So Tailwind-on-bun works, but the integration is a bit rough/unofficial — which is itself a flavor of the compat risk you're trying to escape.
- **CSS Modules, by contrast, is fully native** in `bun build` — zero plugins, zero risk — and already satisfies your scoped/no-clobber requirement.
- On Vite, Tailwind's `@tailwindcss/vite` is the *official first-party* plugin — the smoothest of all.

**Time to converge — here's my recommendation.** Given your actual goals (simplicity, fewer compat surprises) and that this meta-decision has run long:

**Go all-Bun: `bun build` + React + CSS Modules + a global tokens/reset file.** It's the simplest stack, *fully native* (no community plugins to babysit), and meets your hard requirements (scoped, no clobbering). The only concessions vs Panda are sibling-file (not same-file) styles and untyped tokens — ergonomic, not blocking. If you later decide you want utilities, `bun-plugin-tailwind` is a drop-in (with the caveat above), and if it gets rough, the Tailwind CLI is the fallback.

If that lands, I'll write up the concrete migration (Astro → `bun build`): `index.astro` → `index.html` + a React entry, `Poster.astro` → `Poster.tsx`, drop `@astrojs/*` + `astro check` (→ `tsc`, which also lets us unpin TypeScript to 7), keep Bun/Biome/zod/`lib`/tests. Want me to lay that out?

Clear result from the research:

- **StyleX has *official* Bun support** — `@stylexjs/unplugin` with a Bun entrypoint (`@stylexjs/unplugin/bun`) and a [dedicated docs page](https://stylexjs.com/docs/learn/installation/bun). Same-file `stylex.create()`, typed, zero-runtime atomic CSS. This is the elegant integration.
- **Panda has *no* first-class Bun bundler plugin** — its "any bundler" path is a separate `panda codegen` + `panda cssgen` CLI step generating `styled-system/`, which you import. Works, but it's manual orchestration + a generated dir, not a clean plugin.
- **Tailwind** (fallback) — `bun-plugin-tailwind` works (verified earlier), but it's utility strings, not typed css-in-js.

StyleX is the standout. Let me pull the exact Bun setup from its docs, then verify it actually works rather than trust the docs:

Official Bun support, but with real setup detail: production uses a **`Bun.build()` script** with `stylex.esbuild()` (not the plain `bun build` CLI), the documented example uses a **JS entrypoint** (not `index.html` like ours), and dev uses a separate `bunfig.toml` plugin. So the question is whether it integrates cleanly with our **HTML-entrypoint** build. Let me test that empirically:

Concerning — the build "succeeded" but **StyleX generated no CSS** (`rebeccapurple` absent from the output). That matches the docs using a *JS* entrypoint; the HTML-entrypoint flow apparently changes how Bun emits the CSS asset, and the plugin can't append to it. Let me confirm by testing the documented JS-entrypoint path:

Both empirically fall short of "elegant":

- **StyleX** — the official `@stylexjs/unplugin` *installs*, and `Bun.build` reports `success: true`, but **it generated zero CSS** — both with our HTML entrypoint *and* the documented JS-entrypoint approach. The styles just aren't extracted with the config the docs show; getting it working would mean debugging StyleX's `moduleResolution`/plugin config — exactly the compat rabbit hole you're trying to escape. Official-on-paper, not working-in-practice.
- **Panda** — no Bun bundler plugin at all; the only path is orchestrating `panda codegen` + `panda cssgen` CLIs and importing the generated `styled-system/` output. Works, but manual, plus a generated dir. Not elegant.
- **Tailwind** — `bun-plugin-tailwind` I already verified *does* generate CSS cleanly.

So per your instruction, we fall back to **Tailwind**. Two honest things before I wire it in, because one touches your original goal:

1. **Tailwind meets "colocated same-file"** (utility classes live in `className`, no sibling `.module.css`, and it lets us delete `css-modules.d.ts`) — **but it is *not* compile-time typesafe.** Classes are strings; a typo'd `text-gray-500` fails silently (editor plugins autocomplete, but `tsc` won't catch it). So of your two wants — *same-file* and *typesafe* — Tailwind gives you same-file, not typesafe.
2. **It restructures the build slightly**: `bun build ./index.html` (plain CLI) can't take plugins, so `build` becomes a small `scripts/build.ts` (`Bun.build({ plugins: [tailwind] })`), and `dev` needs `bunfig.toml` `[serve.static] plugins = ["bun-plugin-tailwind"]`.

Given #1 — if *typesafe* actually matters more to you than *same-file*, the alternative is staying on **CSS Modules but adding generated per-file types** (typo-safe `styles.month`, still a sibling file). That's the opposite trade: typesafe but not same-file.

Which do you want: **Tailwind** (same-file, untyped — the fallback you authorized), or **typed CSS Modules** (typed, sibling-file)? I'll implement whichever, but wanted the typesafe gap explicit before committing to Tailwind.

Now it's definitive. The full diagnostic:

- Output CSS contains **only** `body { margin: 0 }` (the global) — **no StyleX atomics, no `@layer`, no fallback `stylex.css` anywhere.**
- Yet `stylex.props` is **gone** from the JS bundle — so the transform *ran* (it stripped the StyleX calls), but the extracted CSS **never got emitted**. The styles silently vanish.
- This held across **both** entrypoints, **with** `rootDir`, following the docs exactly.

And it's corroborated upstream: [facebook/stylex #1378 — "Unplugin usage doesn't tap into the standard CSS build pipeline."](https://github.com/facebook/stylex/issues/1378) So this isn't my misconfiguration — **StyleX's Bun integration is broken in practice**: the transform works but the CSS doesn't reach Bun's output. - **Tailwind + Bun** — `bun-plugin-tailwind`, empirically **generates real CSS**. ✅

Yes, it's possible. Two honest caveats on *how*, since they affect authenticity vs. presentability:

**Where the content comes from — two sources:**

- **A) The actual transcript file.** Claude Code stores this session verbatim as a JSONL at `~/.claude/projects/…/<session>.jsonl`. I can read it and convert to markdown — the *real* back-and-forth. (You just interrupted me reaching into `~/.claude`, so I won't go there without your explicit OK.) The raw file also contains my internal reasoning traces and every tool call's full input/output — noisy — so I'd strip the reasoning and trim/summarize tool dumps to make it readable.
- **B) Reconstruct from my context.** I have this whole conversation in context, so I can write it up *without* touching `~/.claude`. Tradeoff: it's my re-rendering, so exact wording (especially yours) may drift slightly from verbatim.

**Presentation — for "demonstrating your process," which shape:**

- **Faithful transcript** — every turn, cleaned up. Authentic but long and includes the messy dead-ends (the CSS/framework thrash), which honestly *is* part of real AI-assisted building.
- **Curated build log / case-study** — a narrative of the arc and decisions (stack choices, the Astro→bun pivot, the CSS saga, TS7, the empirical "test it don't trust it" pattern) with representative excerpts. More compelling as a demonstration, less raw.

**Also worth flagging:** this file gets committed to the repo, so if that repo goes public (GH Pages), the whole conversation becomes public. Nothing sensitive jumped out to me, but it's your call. I'd suggest a path like `docs/build-log.md`.

So, to proceed: **(1)** may I read the `~/.claude` transcript for a verbatim source, or reconstruct from context? And **(2)** faithful transcript or curated build log? My lean for a *demonstration* is a curated build log reconstructed from context — no `~/.claude` access needed, and it reads as a story rather than a 500-turn dump. exchanges.prompt: If we save off the raw JSONL file, is it possible to later strip out the reasoning etc and transform it to md as a build step / even on the fly in React?

steps.text:
Yes to all of it — the JSONL is just one JSON object per line (each a message with typed content blocks: `text`, `thinking`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`), so transforming it is straightforward: parse each line, keep user + assistant `text`, drop (or summarize) the `thinking` and tool blocks, emit markdown. But there's an important difference between the two *when* options:

**Build step (recommended):** a script (`scripts/transcript.ts`) reads the raw JSONL and writes a cleaned `.md` (or a slimmed JSON) at build time. Only the cleaned output ships to the browser. The transform runs once, deterministically, and you can re-run it if you re-export the session.

**On-the-fly in React:** feasible, but the catch is it means **shipping the entire raw JSONL to the client** and stripping in the browser. So the "stripped-out" reasoning, tool dumps, and system prompt are *still downloaded* — anyone opening devtools/network sees them. It's larger and it doesn't actually hide anything. So for anything you want *gone*, do it at build, not on the fly.

**The bigger nuance — committing the raw file:** if you commit the raw JSONL to a repo that goes public (GH Pages), the reasoning traces, the full system prompt, and quite possibly your email (it's injected into the session context) all become public **in the repo and its git history** — regardless of how the *displayed* page strips them. Display-time stripping doesn't help there. So you have three postures:

1. **Commit raw, strip only for display** — full reasoning + PII public in the repo. Fine if that transparency is the point of the demo.
2. **Strip once, commit only the cleaned version** — raw never enters the repo; you keep the raw JSONL elsewhere as your private source.
3. **Commit raw but gitignore it / keep repo private** — raw stays local, generated MD is what's public.

My suggestion: a **build step** that produces the cleaned markdown, and decide up front whether the *raw* JSONL is committed (posture 1) or kept out (posture 2/3). If you want to showcase the reasoning as a feature (a collapsible "AI thinking" section), that's a deliberate keep — just make it an intentional part of the transform, not an accident of shipping the raw file.

How do you want to play it — commit raw + build-step transform, or strip-first-commit-cleaned? And should the cleaned output keep a curated view of the reasoning, or just the conversation?

That flips the decision — **oxlint *does* do Tailwind validation, natively.** Key findings:

- **[`oxlint-tailwindcss`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/oxlint-tailwindcss)** — a *native* oxlint plugin (released March 2026) built **exclusively for Tailwind v4**, with **`no-custom-classname`** (your typo-catcher) plus ~22 other rules (conflicting classes, invalid arbitrary values, deprecated utilities). Native = shares oxlint's parse cycle, zero-config auto-detection of your `@import "tailwindcss"` entry. This is exactly what you want.
- `eslint-plugin-tailwindcss` *also* now supports v4 (via a `cssConfigPath` setting), so ESLint is a viable path too — but it's the slower JS route.

So you **don't** have to fall to ESLint. The all-Rust path you leaned toward works: **oxlint (+ `oxlint-tailwindcss`) for lint, oxfmt for format**, replacing Biome. (I've reverted the `useSortedClasses` Biome edit since sorting isn't the goal.)

Before committing to that migration, though, two real risks worth de-risking empirically first — consistent with how we've vetted everything:

1. **Does `oxlint-tailwindcss` false-flag our SVG arbitrary values?** Our poster is mostly `fill-[#555]`, `text-[13px]`, `[dominant-baseline:middle]` — arbitrary-value/arbitrary-property utilities. If `no-custom-classname` doesn't recognize those as valid, it'll be noise, not help. (Also: typo-catching mostly helps *named* utilities; on arbitrary values there's little to typo — so its value grows as we add real UI, less so on the current SVG.)
2. **oxfmt is beta (0.x)** and its **import sorting** may not express our custom groups (Bun/Node/React carveout → packages → `@/` alias) the way Biome's `organizeImports` does — a possible regression.

My proposal: I run a quick scratchpad test — feed `oxlint-tailwindcss` a real typo (`text-blak-500`) *and* our arbitrary values, confirm it flags the former without false-flagging the latter — and check oxfmt's import-grouping config. exchanges.prompt: It feels weird that oxfmt needs --check but oxlint needs --fix. It feels incongruous. But that's the intended behavior?

steps.text:
It's intended, and the asymmetry actually reflects a real difference in what the two tools *are*, not an oxc inconsistency:

- **A formatter's entire job is to mutate** — "run oxfmt" means "make my files formatted." So writing is the natural default; `--check` is the read-only exception you reach for in CI.
- **A linter's job is to *report*** — "run oxlint" means "tell me what's wrong." Mutation is a *subset* (and not everything is safely auto-fixable), so it's opt-in via `--fix`. Silently rewriting code isn't what you want a linter to do by default.

So each tool defaults to its *primary* action: format defaults to formatting, lint defaults to detecting. Reversed flags, same principle.

It's also a common ecosystem convention, not an oxc quirk — **gofmt** writes by default, and essentially every linter (ESLint, the old Biome lint, oxlint) reports by default with fixing opt-in. The odd one out is actually **Prettier**, which defaults to printing to stdout (needs `--write`); oxfmt chose the gofmt-style write-by-default instead.

The practical upshot is exactly why our scripts look the way they do:
- **CI** wants read-only on both → `oxfmt --check` (flag needed to *not* write) + `oxlint` (already read-only).
- **Fixing** wants mutation on both → `oxfmt` (writes by default) + `oxlint --fix` (flag needed to write).

If the flag-shape bugs you, the mnemonic is: the *bare* command always does the tool's main thing — format formats, lint lints — and you add a flag to get the *other* mode.

exchanges.prompt: Okay, let's move on to the actual content. We want the grid to stream such that when it is in season, it takes up additional space of its neighbors. I think we need to add additional produce to make that work visually? Is that the next step, to get N=5 produce data? Or do you think there's pre-work that we should do before that?

steps.text:
Good instinct that you need more produce — but *researched* data isn't the next step, and the distinction matters:

To develop the streaming **layout**, you need several produce with varied seasons (so there's redistribution to actually see). But that can be **synthetic placeholder** data — 5 fake produce whose spans I pick to stress the layout (a winter crop, a summer crop, a spring ramp, a near-year-rounder, a short pop). *Real* data is a research effort — each produce is a Salinas-Watsonville-style sourcing exercise like strawberries was — and you don't want to sink that time until the layout looks right and the data shape is final. **So: synthetic now, real after the algorithm's nailed.**

The genuine pre-work is the **layout algorithm** — the hard, uncertain part — and it has one fork worth settling before I write geometry:

**How the weekly column is divided.** Each week, produce in season claim height weighted by level (peak = 100, available = 25, absent = 0). The question is the baseline:
- **Normalized** — every week fills the full poster height; ribbons swell and pinch as neighbors come/go. Tidy fixed height. *Downside:* a lone winter crop inflates to the whole height that week, misreading as "tons of it."
- **Absolute** — height = sum of weights, so summer is a tall bulge and winter a thin neck. A true streamgraph — honest, but the top/bottom edges wiggle.
- **Hybrid (my lean)** — mostly absolute (honest proportions) with a floor so lean weeks don't collapse to a sliver.

Two smaller ones I'd fold in:
- **Smoothing** — ribbons should flow, not step jaggedly week to week. That's `d3-shape`'s `area` + a curve interpolator (small, well-worn dep we eyed at the very start). I'd add it rather than hand-roll spline math.
- **Stacking order** — which produce sits where top-to-bottom (by onset? peak week? inside-out?). Affects readability; easy to iterate once it renders.

**Proposed next step:** I write synthetic 5-produce data + a first streamgraph prototype (with `d3-shape`), we look at it, and tune the model live — far faster than debating geometry in the abstract.

The one thing I need to start: **normalized, absolute, or hybrid?** (Or "just pick" — I'll go hybrid and we adjust from the real thing.)

exchanges.prompt: Normalized is definitely out; I agree that the "lone winter crop" is not desirable. I'm very okay with strawberries being a single zero height line when not available; that's the whole point. I would like to move the labeling centered inside the peak span. I think Absolute is correct; we should be distributing the rows with some minimum spacing so that lines stay distinct, but the no availability for that day shrinks and takes up less room. Agree to use d3 built-in math to smooth the steps. As far as the sorting goes, we should pre-sort the produce in order of peak span midpoint ascending. If there's multiple peak spans, choose the widest peak span, and choose the first peak span in the rare tie. That should cause a aesthetically pleasing top-left => bottom-right progression of peaks.

steps.text:
Locked in. Capturing the spec so we're aligned:

- **Absolute** stacking (heights = summed weights; `available`=25, `peak`=100, absent=0), so summer bulges and winter necks down.
- **Minimum inter-ribbon spacing** so lanes stay distinct — and out-of-season pinches to a **zero-height line** (strawberries in winter = a flat line; that's the point).
- **Labels centered inside the peak span** (its midpoint week, in the fat part of the ribbon).
- **Sort order:** by peak-span midpoint ascending; on multiple peak spans use the **widest**, ties broken by the **earliest** — giving a top-left→bottom-right peak diagonal.
- **d3-shape** for the curve smoothing.

Since this is a multi-series data viz, let me load the viz palette guidance before I pick the 5 produce colors, and pull in `d3-shape`:

The skill's key input for us: use a **validated categorical palette in fixed order** for the 5 produce (identity), rather than eyeballed hex. Since art is still deferred, I'll pull the reference palette's categorical hues as accessible placeholders and focus on the geometry. Let me grab those and add `d3-shape`:

The skill's takeaway for a print poster: categorical palette in fixed order for produce identity (height already encodes the seasonality level, so color is pure identity), and skip the interactive/hover layer since this prints. Colors stay placeholder until the art pass. `d3-shape` is in.

Building the four pieces. First the synthetic 5-produce data (peaks spread across the year, including a year-wrapping winter crop to exercise that path):
Now the streamgraph geometry — sort by peak midpoint, per-week absolute stacking with minimum gaps, d3 area paths, labels centered in the peak:
Now the render and pointing App at the sample data:

ci and build both pass (the strict-mode 2D-stacking typechecks clean, all 5 labels in the bundle; the "0 paths" is just my grep — d3 path strings are generated at runtime, not literal in the JS). Per the viz skill's "look at it" step, let me at least sanity-check the geometry numerically — sort order, stacking, label positions:

The geometry is correct — the numeric check confirms the whole design:

| Ribbon (top→bottom) | peak x | peak y |
|---|---|---|
| Meyer Lemon | **21** (far left) | 61 (top) |
| Asparagus | 291 | 75 |
| Strawberries | 498 | 89 |
| Tomatoes | 606 | 114 |
| Winter Squash | **786** (right) | 117 (bottom) |

That's exactly the **top-left → bottom-right peak diagonal** you specified: winter-peaking Meyer Lemon sits top-left, fall-peaking Winter Squash bottom-right, sort order correct, wrap-around peaks handled, all paths non-empty. `ci` + build green.

**What it should render:** 5 stacked ribbons flowing across the year — each swelling to full height at its peak, thinning at `available`, pinching to a flat line when out of season (so a ribbon visibly *streams*), neighbors expanding into the freed space, labels centered in each peak swell.

**View it:** `! bun run dev` → `localhost` (or `! open dist/index.html` after a build).

**Tuning knobs, all in `src/lib/poster/geometry.ts`:**
- `WEIGHT_SCALE` (0.42) — ribbon fatness. The viewBox came out **960×196** (very letterbox, ~5:1); bumping this makes ribbons taller / the poster less squished.
- `ROW_GAP` (14) — spacing between lanes; `CELL_W` (18) — overall width.
- `curveBasis` — the smoothing style (swap for `curveCatmullRom` for a tighter fit to the weekly values).
- `PALETTE` — the placeholder colors (real palette comes with the art pass).

One thing I *can't* judge from numbers is whether it actually reads as flowing streams — label readability, ribbon shape, whether 196px is too short. Want me to spin up the dev server and screenshot it so I can eyeball it with you, or would you rather drive and tell me what to adjust?

exchanges.prompt: [Image #2] This is what it looks like. It's not terrible for a first effort. I didn't realize how much peaks get pushed around: See how Tomatoes gets adjusted so much by Strawberries decline that you can't read the Tomatoes label anymore. In that case, I'd like the peak to not be pushed around, if possible. Also, we shouldn't be collapsing the height of the stream graph; in February, for example, when most produce are out of season, instead of compacting everything near the top, we should distribute the spacing such that the bottom row stays at the bottom. The starting point should be a standard excel-like grid, with the bottom row constant, but at peak times it steals height from its upper siblings. So at any given point, the total height of everything together is consistent. Does that make sense?

steps.text:
That makes sense, and both fixes point at the same change to the layout model. Right now it's top-anchored with a *variable* total, so lean weeks collapse upward and every ribbon's position depends on the full stack above it (which is why Strawberries' decline shoves Tomatoes around).

The fix: **fixed total height, both edges anchored.** I compute the year's fattest week, set the total to that, and then distribute each week's *slack* as equal gaps between rows. Consequences:
- Total height is constant; the bottom row stays put; lean weeks (February) spread into an even Excel-grid instead of collapsing.
- **It also stabilizes peaks** — when a sibling above thins out, its lost height is offset by the gaps growing, so a ribbon barely moves. That directly attacks the Tomatoes-label problem.

Implementing that stacking change:

What changed and what you should see on re-view:
- **February (and other lean stretches)** now spread into an even Excel-grid of thin lines filling the height, rather than compacting to the top with dead space below.
- **The bottom row stays pinned to the bottom** at every week; the total envelope is constant.
- **Peaks are steadier** — when Strawberries thins after its peak, the gaps widen to compensate, so Tomatoes barely shifts. That should make the Tomatoes label sit in its swell again.

2. Is the **Tomatoes** label readable — i.e., did stabilizing the stack put it back in the fat part?

If the label's *still* colliding, the next lever is label placement itself (put it at the ribbon's widest visual point rather than the peak-span midpoint, and/or a faint halo for contrast) — independent of the stacking. And the overall **960×196** is still quite letterbox; `WEIGHT_SCALE` (ribbon fatness) is the knob if you want it taller.

Want to drop another screenshot after you look, or should I spin up the dev server and grab one myself to eyeball alongside you?

steps.text:
That looks great — the diagonal reads clearly, Feb is a clean even grid, and the swells are legible. Nice milestone.

My recommendation: **commit now.** This is a clean, self-contained unit — the whole streaming layout (d3-shape, sort-by-peak, constant-total stacking, the synthetic dev data). It's already a chunky commit, and locking in a known-good state gives us a safe rollback before we start fiddling with aesthetics. Then tweaks become their own focused commit(s), which keeps them reviewable and easy to revert individually if a change doesn't land.

Two things worth flagging before you commit:
- **`App.tsx` currently renders the synthetic `dev-region`, not the real sfbay data** — there's a `TODO` comment marking the swap-back. Just so that's a conscious state going into the commit (the real data only has strawberries, so it can't show the streaming yet).
- One tweak I can already see in your screenshot: **"Meyer Lemon" clips off the left edge** — its peak is at week ~2, so the centered label runs past the left margin. That's a label-placement fix (clamp labels inside the frame, or left-align near edges), independent of the layout.

So my vote is: commit this, then fire the tweak list at me and we'll knock them out as a follow-up. But if you'd rather batch a few in now, I'm happy to — what's on your list? If it's mostly quick aesthetic stuff (label edges, colors, spacing, curve feel) we could reasonably fold a couple in; if it's bigger (interaction, the paper-size frame, real data), those clearly want their own commits.

exchanges.prompt:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The overarching project ("vertumnus", in `~/code/vertumnus`) is to generate a **static, printable web poster** depicting availability and abundance of in-season farmer's-market produce, with **week granularity** (52 weeks, not months) and a **distinction between "available" (25) and "peak" (100, best & cheapest)**. Architecture must support swappable region JSON/data files (first region: SF Bay Area). The user runs all git commands themselves and wants changes left unstaged.

   The most recent and active intent is **the streamgraph poster visualization**: a grid that "streams" so that when produce is in season it takes up additional vertical space from its neighbors. Explicit specification given:
   - **Absolute stacking** (NOT normalized — user rejected normalized due to "lone winter crop" domination). Weights: available=25, peak=100, absent=0.
   - **Zero-height line when out of season** ("strawberries being a single zero height line when not available; that's the whole point").
   - **Fixed total height** — "we shouldn't be collapsing the height... in February... instead of compacting everything near the top, we should distribute the spacing such that the bottom row stays at the bottom. The starting point should be a standard excel-like grid, with the bottom row constant, but at peak times it steals height from its upper siblings. So at any given point, the total height of everything together is consistent."
   - **Peaks should not be pushed around** ("Tomatoes gets adjusted so much by Strawberries decline that you can't read the Tomatoes label anymore. I'd like the peak to not be pushed around, if possible").
   - **Labels centered inside the peak span.**
   - **Sort by peak-span midpoint ascending** — on multiple peak spans use the widest, ties broken by earliest — producing a top-left→bottom-right peak diagonal.
   - **Use d3 built-in math to smooth the steps.**

   The user confirmed the latest result is good and asked whether to commit and tweak as a follow-up, or start tweaking now as part of this commit (has NOT named specific tweaks yet).

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Stack**: Bun's native `bun build` bundler (NOT Astro, NOT Vite) + React 19 SPA (client-rendered), TypeScript 7 (native tsc), Tailwind v4 (via bun-plugin-tailwind), oxlint + oxlint-tailwindcss + oxfmt, zod, d3-shape.
   - **Streamgraph geometry**: absolute stacking with fixed total height; per-week slack distributed as equal inter-ribbon gaps so bottom stays anchored; d3-shape `area()` + `curveBasis` for smooth ribbon paths.
   - **Data model**: zod schemas; weeks 1-52 (1-indexed, canonical 52-week year); year-wrap when to<from; non-overlapping spans validated via `.refine`.
   - **Tailwind class validation**: oxlint-tailwindcss `tailwindcss/no-unknown-classes` catches typos, doesn't false-flag arbitrary values like `fill-[#555]`.
   - **noUncheckedIndexedAccess** (strictest tsconfig) requires `?? 0`/`?? PAD_TOP` guards on array indexing.
   - **Deferred art**: colors are placeholder pending dataviz-skill palette validation.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **src/lib/poster/geometry.ts** (core, most recently edited — the streamgraph geometry):
     - Imports: `import { area, curveBasis } from 'd3-shape';` then `import type { Region } from '@/data/types';` and `import { MONTHS, WEEKS_PER_YEAR } from '@/lib/calendar';`
     - Constants: `LEVEL_WEIGHT: Record<Level,number> = { available: 25, peak: 100 }`, `PAD_X=12, PAD_TOP=40, PAD_BOTTOM=16, CELL_W=18, ROW_GAP=14, WEIGHT_SCALE=0.42`, `GRID_W = WEEKS_PER_YEAR * CELL_W`, `WIDTH = PAD_X*2 + GRID_W`, `PALETTE = ['#2a78d6','#3aa76d','#e0902b','#d1495b','#7a5bd0','#2f9c95','#b5651d']`.
     - Interfaces: `Ribbon { name; color; path; labelX; labelY }`, `PosterModel { width; height; months; ribbons }`.
     - Helpers: `weekToX(week)`, `clamp(v,lo,hi)`, `spanWidth(from,to)` (wrap-aware), `coveredWeeks(from,to)` (wrap-aware), `weeklyWeights(spans): number[]` (52-length, 0-indexed), `peakMidpoint(spans)` (widest peak, earliest tie, wrap-normalized, Infinity if no peak).
     - Module-level: `const areaGen = area<{x;hi;lo}>().x(d=>d.x).y0(d=>d.lo).y1(d=>d.hi).curve(curveBasis);`
     - `buildPoster(region)`: the constant-total layout (most recent change):
       ```ts
       const n = sorted.length;
       const heights = sorted.map((s) => s.weights.map((w) => w * WEIGHT_SCALE));
       const sumPerWeek = Array.from({ length: WEEKS_PER_YEAR }, (_, wk) =>
         heights.reduce((acc, h) => acc + (h[wk] ?? 0), 0));
       const maxSum = Math.max(0, ...sumPerWeek);
       const content = maxSum + Math.max(0, n - 1) * ROW_GAP;
       const height = PAD_TOP + content + PAD_BOTTOM;
       const gapAt = (wk) => (n > 1 ? ROW_GAP + (maxSum - (sumPerWeek[wk] ?? 0)) / (n - 1) : 0);
       const runningTop = new Array<number>(WEEKS_PER_YEAR).fill(PAD_TOP);
       const stacked = sorted.map((item, i) => {
         const h = heights[i] ?? [];
         const samples = [];
         for (let wk = 0; wk < WEEKS_PER_YEAR; wk++) {
           const hi = runningTop[wk] ?? PAD_TOP;
           const lo = hi + (h[wk] ?? 0);
           samples.push({ x: weekToX(wk + 1), hi, lo });
           runningTop[wk] = lo + (i < n - 1 ? gapAt(wk) : 0);
         }
         return { ...item, samples };
       });
       ```
       Then ribbons built with `areaGen(full)` (samples extended to week 53 for full-width fill), labelX=`weekToX(mid)`, labelY=center of ribbon at rounded peak week.
     - Verified: viewBox 960×196, labels spread 61→159 (bottom-anchored constant total).

   - **src/components/Poster.tsx** (renders the SVG):
     ```tsx
     export function Poster({ region }: PosterProps) {
       const model = buildPoster(region);
       return (
     ```

exchanges.prompt: Explain to me this samples concept and what we use it for.

steps.text:
`samples` is the **ribbon's shape, sampled once per week**. Each element is one `Sample` (`Ribbons.tsx:36`):

```ts
interface Sample { x: number; hi: number; lo: number }
```

- `x` — the horizontal position of that week (`weekToX(wk+1)`).
- `hi` — the ribbon's **top** edge (y) that week.
- `lo` — the ribbon's **bottom** edge (y) that week.

(SVG y grows downward, so `hi < lo` numerically, and the ribbon's thickness that week is `lo - hi` — which equals the produce's weight×scale, i.e. 0 when out of season, ~14px available, ~55px peak.)

So one ribbon's `samples` is a 52-element array tracing its top and bottom boundaries across the year — a discrete sampling of an otherwise continuous band.

**How they're built** — in `layout`'s stacking loop (`Ribbons.tsx:157`):

```ts
const hi = runningTop[wk] ?? PAD_TOP;   // top = wherever the ribbons above ended
const lo = hi + (h[wk] ?? 0);           // bottom = top + this week's thickness
samples.push({ x: weekToX(wk + 1), hi, lo });
runningTop[wk] = lo + gap;              // advance the cursor for the next ribbon down
```

`runningTop` is a per-week cursor that walks down the stack; each ribbon claims a `[hi, lo]` slice and pushes the cursor lower. That's what makes the streamgraph stack.

**What we use them for — two things:**

1. **Drawing the ribbon** (`Ribbons.tsx:173`). d3's `areaGen` reads `x`, `y1=hi`, `y0=lo` from each sample and interpolates them with `curveBasis` into the smooth filled `<path>`. The samples *are* the geometry the curve is fit through. (`full` is just `samples` plus one extra point at week 53 so the fill reaches the right edge — `Ribbons.tsx:166`.)

2. **Placing the label vertically** (`averageCenter`, `Ribbons.tsx:183`). To center a label on the peak's visual middle, we average each week's vertical midline `(hi + lo)/2` over the weeks near the peak midpoint where the ribbon is actually present (`lo - hi > 0`). Sampling several weeks instead of one is what stops the label from jumping as the band flows up and down.

In short: `layout` computes the stacked band as weekly `samples`; the path renderer turns them into the visible ribbon, and `RibbonLabel` reads them back to sit the text in the right vertical spot. The name comes from d3's mental model — you hand the area generator a series of sample points and it draws the curve between them.

exchanges.prompt: Okay. Is there a better name for samples? I'm okay with it, but it wasn't immediately obvious to me what they were.

steps.text:
Yeah — `samples` is d3's vocabulary (you hand an area generator a series of sample points), but it leaks an implementation detail instead of saying what the thing *is*. Each element is really **one week's vertical slice of the ribbon** — a top edge, a bottom edge, at an x.

My recommendation: rename `samples` → **`slices`** and the `Sample` type → **`Slice`**. Then the code reads as "a ribbon is a series of vertical slices," and the two use sites explain themselves:

```ts
interface Slice { x: number; top: number; bottom: number }
// ...
areaGen(fullSlices)              // draw the band through the slices
averageCenter(slices, midIdx)    // label sits at the slices' vertical midline
```

I'd also fold in a companion rename while we're here: **`hi`/`lo` → `top`/`bottom`**. `hi`/`lo` reads as high/low *value*, but they're screen positions (and confusingly `hi` is the smaller y). `top`/`bottom` is unambiguous, and thickness becomes the obvious `bottom - top`.

Alternatives if `slices` doesn't land for you:
- **`band`** — "the ribbon is a band; draw it through these points" (`areaGen(band)` reads nicely, but a single word for an array is a little odd).
- **`weeklyBounds`** — most literal, bit verbose.
- **`outline`** — accurate-ish, but usually implies one closed path rather than per-week points.

Want me to apply `slices` + `top`/`bottom`? It's a mechanical rename across `layout`, `averageCenter`, `areaGen`, and the `Ribbon`/`Slice` types — no behavior change.

exchanges.prompt: Yes, let's do slice + top/bottom. Ideally, there's a single transformation where we take spans and convert them into slices and thereafter hide spans, but I don't think we have to be quite so academic here. Some denormalization seems fine.

steps.text:
The rename is done and verified — CI green, 9 tests pass, and the render is **byte-identical** (154176 bytes) to before, confirming it's a pure rename.

Summary of what changed in `Ribbons.tsx`:
- `Sample` → **`Slice`** (with a doc comment: "One week's vertical slice of a ribbon…"), `samples` → **`slices`**.
- `hi`/`lo` → **`top`/`bottom`** throughout (`areaGen` now reads `.y0(bottom).y1(top)`, thickness is the obvious `bottom - top`).
- `full` → `fullSlices` for consistency.

And per your note, I kept `spans` on the `Ribbon` alongside `slices` — the denormalization is harmless and avoids contorting `layout` into a single spans→slices funnel just for purity's sake. `RibbonLabel` still needs `spans` (for the peak geometry) and `slices` (for vertical placement), and both being present reads fine.

Before I build this, a genuine recommendation on the library question — because it shapes what I install.

This banner is a small, self-contained interaction: open by default, dismiss to a floating reopen button. That's `useState` + Tailwind, ~30 lines, and it stays consistent with how the rest of the app is built. **shadcn** and **Chakra** are both a meaningful commitment on *this* stack (bun's native bundler + Tailwind v4, deliberately lean deps):
- **shadcn** isn't a package — its CLI scaffolds Radix-based components and assumes a Vite/Next + specific Tailwind setup; on bun build + Tailwind v4 you'd be adapting its config, and it pulls Radix deps.
- **Chakra** ships its *own* styling engine, which duplicates Tailwind, adds runtime weight, and can fight bun's bundler.

The real case for a library isn't this banner — it's the *next* interactive pieces (a region dropdown, the chart's hover tooltips from the dataviz pass, any modal). Those benefit from accessible primitives. So my instinct is: build the banner plain now, and adopt a library when a component actually needs a11y primitives — and when we do, prefer headless + Tailwind-friendly (Radix or Ark) over shadcn's CLI or Chakra.

But it's your call since it sets a precedent:

- **What the plain build actually looks like** (the ~30 lines, the a11y I'd include by hand, and what we'd *give up* vs a primitives library).
- **The concrete cost of shadcn or Chakra on this stack** — the exact setup friction with bun build + Tailwind v4, what deps land, bundle impact.
- **The forward-looking view** — which interactive components we actually expect (region picker, chart hover tooltips, modals) and which library best serves them, so we're not choosing for a banner in isolation.
- Or if your question is more like *"why not just pick one now and standardize"* — I can make the case for committing early vs. deferring.

steps.text:
That list actually settles it — let me map each control to what it needs:

| Control | What it really is | Accessible primitive needed? |
|---|---|---|
| **Region picker** | a select | Native `<select>` — keyboard nav, mobile, a11y all free |
| **Paper size picker** | a select + reveal 2 number inputs on "Custom" | Native `<select>` + `<input type="number">` |
| **Custom aspect ratio** | width × height inputs | Native inputs |
| **Print button** | `onClick={() => window.print()}` | Native `<button>` |
| **Dismissible banner** | `useState` toggle + two buttons | Native `<button>` |

**Every one of these is a native, already-accessible HTML element.** The whole expected surface is form controls and buttons — not the rich component ecosystem (modals with focus traps, comboboxes, command palettes) that shadcn/Chakra exist to provide. So a component library here buys us essentially nothing functional, while costing real setup work on bun build + Tailwind v4, new deps, and a bigger bundle on what's meant to be a lean static-Pages poster.

The single thing a library *would* add is prettier custom-styled dropdowns (a native `<select>`'s open list uses OS styling you can't fully theme). If that bothers us later, we drop in **one** headless primitive (Radix Select) for that one control, in isolation — no framework-wide commitment. That's a reversible, à-la-carte decision, not a foundation.

steps.text:
This is a fair case where a library genuinely earns its keep — and it's a *different* category from the shadcn/Chakra discussion. Those are **component** libraries for form UI, which we still don't need (native controls cover the pickers/buttons). This is an **animation** need, and a declarative *shared-element morph* — centered card ⇄ bottom-right icon — is exactly the thing that's painful to hand-roll but trivial with the right tool.

**Recommendation: Framer Motion (the `motion` package).** With it, the Banner becomes two `motion` elements sharing a `layoutId="banner"` inside `AnimatePresence`, and Framer automatically animates the morph between the centered modal and the corner icon — position, size, and corner-radius all interpolate, so you literally see it fly to/from the corner. That's the "people understand where it went and how to get it back" behavior, declaratively. It's ~30–50KB gzipped — the one real cost on an otherwise tiny bundle — and it's styling-agnostic (plays fine with Tailwind) and bundler-agnostic (works with bun build).

The no-dep alternative is plain CSS transitions, but the morph specifically — animating from flex-centered to fixed-corner while swapping the contents — is what CSS does *poorly*. You'd get a passable fade+scale, not a clean "it flew to the corner." Since the whole point is the spatial cue, I'd spend the ~40KB here rather than settle for the weaker effect.

So my plan: add `motion`, center the open modal, and wire the `layoutId` morph between the two states (still driven by the `hideBanner` URL param).

Right now "default false" is **implicit**: when `hideBanner` is absent, the input is `undefined`, the `z.enum([...]).transform(...)` chain fails to parse it, and `.catch(false)` swallows that failure into `false`. So `.catch(false)` is silently doing double duty — "malformed value → false" *and* "absent → false" — and nowhere does it *say* "the default is false." That should be explicit.

Let me verify how zod v4 handles an explicit `.default()` on that transform pipe before I rewrite it (the `.default`/`.catch` interaction has v4-specific nuances):

No more relying on `.catch` to silently mean "default."

**2. The open modal is centered in the viewport** (`top-1/2 left-1/2 -translate-x/y-1/2`), both axes. I used transform-centering rather than a full-screen flex overlay, so there's no invisible layer intercepting clicks to the poster behind it. The dismissed state (bottom-right "i") is unchanged.

exchanges.prompt: Explain the backgroundColor animation. Is that needed?

steps.text:
It's the mechanism that keeps the green from showing up too early — so yes, it's needed for the behavior you approved.

Here's the chain of reasoning:

- With `layoutId`, the **icon** is the element that travels/shrinks from the card's center position to the corner. So whatever the icon *looks like* is what you see moving during the morph.
- If the icon just had a static `bg-green-700` class, that traveling box would be green the entire way — which is exactly the "it instantly becomes the green icon and slides down" problem you rejected earlier.
- Instead, I removed the green class and **animate the background from white (`#ffffff`, matching the card) → green (`#15803d`)** on the `revealLate` timing (delayed to 80% through). So the box stays white — reads as the card — for the whole travel, and only flips to green at the tail. It's the color half of "morph to the icon *at the end*"; the `<motion.span>` opacity on the "i" is the content half, on the same timing.

Two consequences worth noting:
- The `initial={{ backgroundColor: '#ffffff' }}` matters too — without a green class *and* without an initial, the box would have no background (transparent) mid-morph and blink. White initial keeps it opaque and card-like.
- Since there's no `bg-green-700` class anymore, this `animate` value is also what defines the **resting** green of the icon (that's why the direct-load screenshot was correctly green).

So if we deleted the `backgroundColor` animation, we'd have to re-add a static green class, and we'd be back to a green box traveling to the corner. The only real alternative that keeps the "neutral while traveling" look would be a fixed neutral color instead of matching white — but white (matching the card) is what makes the morph seamless. I'd keep it.

exchanges.prompt: What's the difference between ISC and MIT?

steps.text:
Both are OSI-approved **permissive** licenses, and for practical purposes they're interchangeable — same freedoms, same single obligation on you. The differences are mostly in wording:

**What's the same (the part that matters for us):**
- Use, modify, distribute, commercial use — all allowed.
- The only requirement: **retain the copyright notice + license text** in copies you distribute.
- No warranty, no liability, no copyleft. Both are GPL-compatible.

**Where they differ:**
1. **Length.** ISC is deliberately shorter. It was written (by the Internet Systems Consortium, used by OpenBSD) as a "trimmed MIT/BSD" — removing language considered legally redundant after the Berne Convention (e.g. you don't need to explicitly assert copyright).
2. **The permission grant.** MIT enumerates verbs — "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell." ISC condenses that to "use, copy, modify, and/or distribute … for any purpose with or without fee." The omitted verbs are considered subsumed, so it's the same grant, just fewer words.
3. **Noninfringement.** MIT's warranty disclaimer explicitly includes **"NONINFRINGEMENT"** (i.e. no promise the code doesn't infringe someone else's IP). ISC's disclaimer doesn't name it. This is the one genuinely substantive wording gap, and it's minor/rarely consequential.

**Bottom line for the project:** zero practical difference to how we comply — both go in the same acknowledgements list with their copyright + text. Your original "MIT" requirement was really "permissive with attribution," and ISC satisfies that identically. (Not legal advice, just the general shape of it.)

steps.name: WebSearch
steps.detail: Tailwind CSS v4 button cursor pointer removed default preflight controversy

steps.text:
Both verified.

**1. The cursor change is real — and yes, notoriously controversial.** In Tailwind **v4** (since v4.0.0-alpha.22), Preflight no longer sets `cursor: pointer` on buttons; they fall back to the native `cursor: default`. It was contentious enough to spawn a discussion literally titled *"Silent removal of cursor: pointer on `<button>`"* — the "silent" part being a big complaint, since it wasn't in the upgrade guide initially and broke shadcn/ui expectations. Adam Wathan's rationale (in the PR): the hand/pointer cursor is semantically meant for **links**, native OS buttons don't use it, and "UI-forward" apps like Linear use the default cursor — so they nudged the ecosystem that way. Plenty of people disagree, which is why the standard fix is exactly the base-layer snippet we added.

**2. Yes — `@import 'tailwindcss'` includes the reset automatically.** Let me show you the precise structure:
Interesting — `index.css` has no `@import` lines, just the layer declaration. So let me confirm how Preflight gets in (inlined vs. engine-injected) to give you an accurate answer:

Both fully confirmed:

**1. The cursor change is real and was genuinely controversial.** Verified in Tailwind's own tracker — the flagship thread is even titled *"Silent removal of `cursor: pointer`"*. The "silent" framing is the crux of the controversy: it shipped without being in the v4 upgrade guide and quietly broke every button in projects (shadcn/ui especially). Adam Wathan's stated reasoning in the PR: `cursor: pointer` is semantically for **links**, native OS buttons don't use a hand cursor, and design-led apps (Linear) use the default — so Tailwind deliberately nudged the ecosystem. Lots of people push back on it, which is why "add it back in a base layer" is the near-universal fix.

**2. Yes — `@import 'tailwindcss'` includes the reset automatically; you don't add normalize yourself.** I traced it: the bare `tailwindcss` specifier resolves (via its `"style": "./index.css"` export) to `index.css`, which **inlines Preflight** in the `base` layer (I grepped it — the box-sizing / `appearance: button` reset rules are right there) and ends with `@tailwind utilities`. Preflight *is* Tailwind's reset — a normalize-derived cross-browser layer plus opinionated resets (zeroed margins, reset borders, unstyled headings/lists, etc.). So it both normalizes and resets, in one import.

The neat irony: that's *exactly why the cursor thing bit us* — Preflight is active, and Preflight is what stopped setting the button cursor. If you ever wanted to opt out of the reset you'd import the layers à la carte (`theme` + `utilities`, skip `preflight`) — but for this app you want it.

Sources:
- [Discussion #18182 — "Silent removal of cursor: pointer on `<button>`"](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/discussions/18182)
- [Issue #15773 — Default button style missing pointer cursor](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/issues/15773)
- [PR #8962 — "Don't use cursor: pointer for buttons by default" (adamwathan)](https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss/pull/8962)

Confirmed the mechanism works (probe output above): with a build-time `define`, Bun constant-folds `typeof __APP_BASE__ === 'undefined' ? '/' : __APP_BASE__` down to `var BASE = "/vertumnus/"` in prod, and in dev the guarded free identifier safely evaluates to `'/'`. So the base can be one build-time knob.

**The nice simplifier:** you don't need `publicPath` at all. The build emits *relative* asset paths (`./chunk.js`), and the browser resolves `./` against the directory of the current URL — which for a **single-segment** route is always the base:
- `/vertumnus/sfbay` → `./chunk.js` = `/vertumnus/chunk.js` ✓
- `/vertumnus/` → `/vertumnus/chunk.js` ✓
- `/sfbay` (root deploy) → `/chunk.js` ✓

The only thing that would break relative assets is a trailing slash or a *second* path segment — and we control the links, so region stays a single segment with no trailing slash.

**So the project-page solution is three pieces** (on top of the code seam we agreed — shared location core + sibling region helper + `RegionPicker` + swapping `App` off `testRegion`):

3. **Base-aware router.** Read = strip `BASE` off `location.pathname`, take the first segment, validate against `REGION_IDS` (else default). Write = `pathname = BASE + id`.

Flipping between deploy targets is then **one constant**: `BASE = '/'` (dev + custom-domain/user-page) vs `'/vertumnus/'` (project page). Dev is unaffected either way.

exchanges.prompt: Hmm, routing logic being hidden in region.ts is a code smell. What would it take to have a true directory based routing system, where we define the route by adding a /pages/sfbay.tsx or /pages/sfbay/index.tsx file?
