If you see a path forward there I'm up for moving to that architecture. One thing to note that even though it is meant to be printed, I do have a notion of adding hover tooltips to the web version for source visibility and details, though of course those won't show up in the print version.

steps.text: Let me look up the Astro issue in the history:

Found it — the history confirms your memory: **Astro is Vite-based and "developed and tested Node-first,"** and running it under Bun was "the less-trodden path." That was a reasonable call, and **nothing I'm proposing requires going back** — what you'd want from Astro here is one function call (`renderToStaticMarkup`), not a framework.

## The resizing question — there's a clean path, and it's simpler than what we have

The key realization: **the layout depends only on the aspect ratio, never on pixel size.** We measure pixels today only because `viewBox` is set to the measured box so 1 unit = 1 px. That constraint is self-imposed.

Instead, set the viewBox in *paper units*:

```
viewBox = "0 0 1000 ${1000 * h / w}"     // Letter 11×8.5 → "0 0 1000 773"
```

The container already has `aspect-ratio: w/h`, so the SVG scales **uniformly** to fill it. SVG is vector — text stays crisp at any scale. The earlier concern about stretched text applied to *non-uniform* scaling; uniform scaling is exactly what you want.

So: **`ResizeObserver`, `useLayoutEffect`, the size state, and the first-paint flash all disappear.** Window resizing no longer triggers any JS — the browser just scales vectors. And you get the proportional label font you deferred, for free, because labels now scale with the poster (which is also more faithful: the preview matches the print).

**Arbitrary dimensions still work** — a custom size is just a different aspect ratio, so the layout recomputes as pure math (microseconds, no measurement). What changes is only *when* it runs:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Default paper (Letter)** | pre-rendered at build time → poster visible instantly, no JS |
| **Any other size** | client recomputes the SVG from bundled data |

For the CSS chrome (sage frame, title) to scale with it, use **container query units** — `container-type: size` on the poster and sizes in `cqw` instead of fixed `p-8`/`text-3xl`. Then frame, title, and chart all scale together at any paper size, still with zero JS.

One honest limit: filling an arbitrary aspect ratio without distortion genuinely requires per-aspect layout, so you can't pre-render *every* size. Pre-rendering the default (or the ~6 presets) covers the common path; custom sizes fall back to client render. That's normal progressive enhancement, not a compromise.

## Tooltips fit this fine

They're pure enhancement and don't conflict with static-first: attach one delegated listener to the pre-rendered SVG (ribbon paths carry a `data-produce` attribute), show a positioned div, and `@media print { … display: none }`. The poster still works without JS; tooltips appear when it loads. They're also an argument for keeping React around for the interactive layer — which I'm not proposing to remove.

## The banner animation — you can keep the effect and drop the 44 KB

Your reasoning was sound: the morph teaches users *where the banner went*. The native replacement is the **View Transitions API**:

```js
document.startViewTransition(() => setHidden(true));
```

with `view-transition-name: banner` on both the card and the icon. The browser morphs position and size between them — the same "card travels to the corner and becomes the icon" affordance, no library. It degrades to an instant swap on browsers without support, which is a graceful floor.

That's arguably *more* elegant than the Framer version, since it also removes the timing coupling you had to hand-tune (`revealLate`, the `whileHover` regression).

## What I'd propose

**Step 1 — the viewBox change.** Self-contained, deletes code, gains proportional fonts, and unlocks everything else. Low risk, and I can verify it visually against the current output.

**Step 2 — the cheap wins:** `NODE_ENV=production`, drop runtime zod, swap motion for View Transitions. Should land ~190 KB → ~70 KB gzipped.

**Step 3 — build-time pre-render**, once Step 1 makes the poster a pure function of (region, aspect).

I'd start with Step 1 alone so you can see the poster before/after and confirm proportional labels look right — that's the one change with a visible design consequence, and if you dislike it, nothing else is blocked. Want me to do that?

exchanges.prompt: Okay, let's do the viewBox change. Though I want to confirm that this will work with the non SVG border. The Ribbons SVG itself isn't 11x8.5; the poster is 11x8.5, which has a border around it, and the SVG is some smaller dimension within that.

steps.text:
Sharp catch — that's exactly the crux, and it exposes a related issue in the current design.

Today the chrome is **fixed pixels**: `p-8` (32px frame), `text-3xl` (30px title), `mt-6`, `p-3`. So the chart box aspect isn't the paper aspect — it's paper minus fixed padding. That works now *only because* we measure the chart box. It also means printing A5 vs A3 gives you the same 32px border, which is proportionally huge on one and thin on the other — the chrome doesn't currently scale with the paper at all.

So there are two ways to make the chart's aspect derivable without measuring:

**Option A — proportional CSS chrome.** Express the frame/title as *fractions* rather than pixels, then the chart box aspect follows arithmetically:

```
posterW = 1000,  posterH = 1000 * h/w
frame   = 0.035 * posterW
titleH  = 0.10  * posterH
chartW  = posterW - 2*frame
chartH  = posterH - titleH - frame     →  viewBox = "0 0 chartW chartH"
```

Same constants drive both the CSS (as percentages/`cqw`) and the layout math, so they can't disagree. Keeps Tailwind styling the poster. The risk is drift — if CSS and the math ever diverge, the SVG letterboxes slightly inside its box.

**Option B — put the whole poster in the SVG.** One `viewBox` at the paper aspect containing the sage `<rect>`, the title `<text>`, the white rounded card `<rect rx>`, and the ribbons. **This dissolves your concern entirely** — there's no CSS/SVG boundary to keep in sync, because there's no boundary.

I lean **B**, for reasons specific to this being a print product:
- One coordinate system → the printed output is exact by construction, not by two systems agreeing
- The whole poster becomes a pure function of `(region, aspect)` — ideal for the build-time pre-render, and it makes "download as SVG/PDF" nearly free later
- It fixes the fixed-px chrome problem automatically
- The chrome is genuinely small: a background rect, a title, a rounded card — ~15 lines. We already render SVG text, and we already have `wrapWords` for the planned footer citations

The trade: Tailwind no longer styles the poster interior (it still styles the app shell and banner), and SVG text has no auto-wrapping — which matters mainly for the future footer, where we'd reuse `wrapWords`. The outer drop shadow stays CSS on the wrapper, since it's screen-only decoration.

Both are real options and A is a smaller diff. **Which do you want?** If you say B I'll move the frame and title into the SVG; if A, I'll keep the CSS chrome and make it proportional.

exchanges.prompt: Hmm, I'm unfamiliar with SVG CSS; I was thinking for the title and footer it would be nice to have flexbox ergonomics like align-items center and justify-content middle. If we can do similar things in SVG elegantly, I'm not opposed to making everything SVG.

steps.text:
Honest answer: **single-line centering is genuinely one attribute in SVG** — often cleaner than the CSS. What you lose is *content-driven* layout, but a poster has three fixed bands, so there's little to lose.

| CSS | SVG equivalent |
|---|---|
| `justify-content: center` | `text-anchor="middle"` with `x={W/2}` |
| `align-items: center` | `dominant-baseline="central"` with `y={bandCenter}` |
| `flex-grow` / `gap` | computed constants |
| text wrapping | manual — but we already have `wrapWords` |

The clincher: **Option A needs that same arithmetic anyway.** To derive the chart's aspect without measuring, you must subtract the title and footer bands regardless — Option A just forces you to *also* express it in CSS and keep the two in sync. So all-SVG doesn't add math; it removes a duplicate.

Here's the shape it takes:

```tsx
<text x={W / 2} y={TITLE_H / 2} textAnchor="middle" dominantBaseline="central">
  {region.name}
</text>
```

(One caveat I'd avoid: `<foreignObject>` *can* embed real HTML+flexbox inside SVG, but its print fidelity is inconsistent across browsers — a bad bet for a print-first product.)

Let me read the current files and build it:

Now `Ribbons` becomes a `<g>` — the measuring machinery goes away entirely:
Let me make the poster SVG fully self-contained (no Tailwind dependency inside it, which matters for the future pre-render/export):
Now the visual check — the real test is whether it looks right and whether labels scale proportionally:
Letter renders identically to before. Now the real tests — a very different aspect, and a narrow viewport:

The narrow-viewport shot is the proof: at 420px the **entire poster scales down uniformly** — frame, title, month axis, and ribbon labels all shrink together, so it's a faithful miniature of what prints. That's the "what you see is what prints" property we were after.

The viewBox change is done and verified. CI green (37 tests).

**What went away:** `ResizeObserver`, `useLayoutEffect`, `useRef`, `useState`, the size-gate, the two-component split, and the initial-paint flash. `Ribbons` is now a pure function of `(items, width, height)` returning a `<g>` — no hooks at all. **`buildStreamgraph` and all its helpers were untouched**; they just receive poster units instead of pixels.

**To your border question — it resolved cleanly.** The whole poster is now one SVG at the paper aspect (`viewBox="0 0 1000 773"` for Letter): sage `<rect>`, title `<text>`, white rounded card `<rect rx>`, then the chart in a `<g transform>`. No CSS/SVG boundary to keep in sync.

The SVG ergonomics turned out fine, as hoped — the title is exactly the one-liner:
```tsx
<text x={POSTER_W / 2} y={FRAME + TITLE_H / 2} textAnchor="middle" dominantBaseline="central">
```

I also converted the remaining Tailwind classes inside the poster (`fill-white`, `text-[11px]`) to SVG attributes, so **the poster SVG is fully self-contained** — no external CSS needed. That matters for the build-time pre-render, and it makes "download as SVG" nearly free later.

**Verified across aspects:** Letter renders essentially identically to before (the old px constants carried over as poster units, since the poster was ~1000px wide anyway), Tabloid and Portrait reshape correctly, and the narrow viewport scales everything proportionally.

**One thing I noticed worth a follow-up, not a blocker:** a portrait poster overflows the viewport vertically — the SVG is `w-full max-w-5xl`, so height follows the aspect and can exceed the screen. It should probably also be constrained by viewport height (`max-h-[…vh]` with `w-auto`) so tall posters fit. Want me to fix that now, or leave it with the rest of the follow-ups?

The remaining items from the review are unchanged and independent: `NODE_ENV=production`, dropping runtime zod, swapping motion for View Transitions, then the build-time pre-render (which this change just unblocked).

**Everything in this change, together:**
- Poster is one self-contained SVG at the paper's aspect (`viewBox="0 0 1000 {1000·h/w}"`) — frame, title, card, and chart in one coordinate system, no CSS/SVG boundary

steps.text: Correct on both counts. Let me confirm rather than assert:

Confirmed on both counts. **Still fully client-rendered.** The built `dist/index.html` body is just `
` — zero poster markup. Everything still paints only after React boots. No pre-render was done. **Preset and custom sizes are the identical codepath.** `Poster` reads `const { w, h } = useQueryParams()` and computes `posterH = POSTER_W * h / w`. Nothing anywhere branches on "is this a preset?" — a preset click just writes `w`/`h` params, exactly like typing custom dimensions. `matchPaperSize()` only exists to *label* the current size in the UI ("Letter" vs "Custom"); it has no effect on rendering. So what this change actually bought is **the precondition** for going static, not the static rendering itself: the poster is now a pure function of `(region, w, h)` with no DOM measurement, so it *can* be computed at build time. Previously it couldn't be, because it depended on measuring a live element. When we do the pre-render, that shared codepath is what makes it clean: build time calls the same function with the default paper size and inlines the result; the client only re-renders when `w`/`h` differ from what was baked in. One implementation, two invocation sites. Nothing here changes behavior for users yet — it's the same client render, just simpler and now scale-correct. Good to commit.

steps.text:
Checked, and here's the honest picture — with the caveat that the big change landed *after* my cutoff, so this is from search, not memory.

**What actually changed:** [Vite 8 went stable on March 12, 2026](https://www.nexgismo.com/blog/vite-8-rolldown-migration-guide-2026) with **Rolldown** (VoidZero's Rust bundler) integrated, unifying dev and prod builds. Vite remains "the recommended bundler for 99% of teams." And the commonly recommended 2026 setup is [**Bun as package manager + script runner, Vite as the bundler**](https://www.pkgpulse.com/guides/bun-vs-vite-2026) — with one pointed caveat about Bun's bundler specifically: *"it's too early to trust the built-in bundler."*

So the ecosystem did move, and there's a real mainstream position that isn't what we're doing.

**That said — yes, `bun build` is still reasonable here, and I'd stay.** Three reasons specific to this project:

1. **The bundler isn't what's making our bundle big.** 190 KB gzipped is dominated by *what we import* — zod (~63 KB) and motion (~44 KB) are over half of it. Dropping those beats any realistic tree-shaking difference between bundlers. Swapping bundlers now would be churn aimed at the wrong lever.

2. **Our build is the simplest case that exists**: one entry HTML, one plugin (Tailwind), minify, static output. That's exactly where "too early to trust" carries least weight — we're not exercising code-splitting, SSR, module federation, or a plugin chain. Our `build.ts` is 25 lines.

3. **The pre-render is *easier* on Bun.** Step 4 on the roadmap is calling `renderToStaticMarkup` at build time and inlining the result. In `build.ts` that's just Bun running our own code — no plugin, no framework hook. Under Vite it'd be a plugin or a separate SSG step.

And we already get the oxc dividend — `oxlint` and `oxfmt` are from that same Rust toolchain — without adopting Vite.

**When I'd revisit:** if you want the plugin ecosystem, file-based routing (which we evaluated and rejected), or hit a real bundler limitation. The migration path is well-trodden and we'd keep Bun as runtime and package manager either way, so it's a reversible decision, not a lock-in.

I could *measure* it — stand up a Vite+Rolldown build of the same source and compare output size — but I'd expect the delta to be small next to removing zod and motion, so I'd rather do those first and re-measure. Say the word if you want the comparison anyway.

Want me to pick crop discovery back up? I had just found what the Fresno reports actually carry: **fruit** — avocados, strawberries, grapes, kiwifruit, nectarines, peaches, blueberries, pomegranates, plums, cherries, raspberries, blackberries; **vegetables** — only sweet potatoes and asparagus, which is thin and probably means the veg data needs a different report.

Excellent — that changes things. Two genuinely better options:

- **San Francisco Terminal Market Vegetables (`SX_FV020`, slug 2323)** — the actual SF wholesale produce market. Discontinued, but it ran through **May 1, 2025**, so there's recent multi-year data. Seasonality is stable year-to-year, so a 2022–2025 window is perfectly usable.

Very promising — the schema has **`origin`** and **`district`**, and **53,485 of the rows are California-origin**. Let me analyze the cached file offline:

**Found it — 107 California-origin vegetables** at the San Francisco terminal market. Everything a farmers' market poster needs:

> artichokes · asparagus · broccoli · brussels sprouts · cabbage · carrots · cauliflower · celery · sweet corn · cucumbers · eggplant · fava beans · garlic · kale/chard/collard/mustard/dandelion greens · leeks · lettuces · snow & sugar snap peas · peppers · pumpkins · radishes · spinach · squashes (zucchini, butternut, acorn, delicata, kabocha, spaghetti) · tomatoes (incl. cherry, grape, plum) · turnips …

And the districts confirm your instinct about relevance: **Salinas-Watsonville**, **Central Coast**, **Salinas Valley** — the Bay Area's actual growing regions, not Southern California.

**Three caveats worth knowing before we dive deep:**

1. **The API caps responses at 100,000 rows.** My one-year request silently truncated to Apr 5 – Dec 31, 2024 (124 MB!). Full years need windowed pulls — but per-commodity queries are tiny, so this only affects discovery, not the real pulls.
2. **The report was discontinued May 1, 2025**, so the usable window is roughly 2022–2025. Fine for seasonality (it's stable year over year), but the citation should say so plainly.
3. **It's terminal (wholesale arrival) data, not shipping-point (harvest) data** — a slightly different measurement than our cherries.

```

```

Peak weeks 21–26 is plausible (~a week after the harvest-side 20–24, exactly the terminal lag you predicted). But **weeks 31–33 and 51 are noise** — California cherries aren't in season in August or late December. This is precisely the "stray listings become spurious spans" case I documented in `season.test.ts`. Let me look at the actual distribution (offline):

Now the picture is clear — and it points at a principled fix:

- **Main season: weeks 17–26**, a clean curve peaking at wk 24 (118 listings)
- **Weeks 31–33 are *only* August 2022**; **week 51 is *only* December 2023**

So the noise is **single-year anomalies**, while real seasonality recurs every year. That's a much better discriminator than a raw threshold. Let me verify that holds across all weeks:

Perfect discrimination:

| weeks | years seen |
|---|---|
| 17–26 (real season) | **2–3 years** |
| 31, 32, 33, 51 (noise) | **exactly 1 year each** |

So the rule is: **a week only counts if it recurs across multiple years.** That's principled rather than an arbitrary magnitude cutoff — and importantly it preserves genuine low-volume shoulders (week 17 has just 1 listing per year, but appears in two years), while a percentage floor would have deleted them. It also handles legitimate double seasons (figs' breba + main crop) correctly, since a real second season recurs annually.
Now tests for the new rule, then re-derive (no API call — reuses the cache):
Derivation is clean now (`available 17-20, peak 21-26` — noise gone), but I got test week-numbers wrong. Let me see:

My date arithmetic was off — and the reason is worth noting: **leap years shift the same calendar date into a different week** (`05/06/2023` → wk 18, `05/06/2024` → wk 19, since day-of-year shifts by one). Let me use non-leap pairs so the tests are unambiguous:

Cherries are now on the terminal methodology, clean. CI green (41 tests, +4 new).

**Result:** `available` wk 17–20 (Apr 23 – May 20), `peak` wk 21–26 (May 21 – Jul 1). The spurious August-2022 and December-2023 spans are gone, and the citation now self-documents the report, the California-grown filter, the seasons used, and the May 2025 discontinuation.

**The methodology change that made it work:** terminal data is noisier than shipping-point, so I added a **multi-year recurrence filter** — a week only counts if it appears in ≥2 cached seasons. On the cherry data that separated signal from noise perfectly (real weeks appeared in 2–3 years; every noise week in exactly 1). I chose it over a magnitude threshold because a percentage floor would have deleted week 17, a genuine season-start with only one listing per year. It also handles real double seasons (figs' breba + main crop) correctly, since those recur annually. There's a guard so a single cached season isn't wiped out.

Two things worth carrying forward as we scale:
- **Leap years shift a date's week by one** (day-of-year ÷ 7), so identical calendar dates can land in adjacent buckets. Harmless at ±1 week for seasonality, but it bit my test fixtures, and the tests now document it.
- **Terminal data needs 3+ years** for the recurrence filter to be meaningful — I used 2022–2025 here rather than the old 3-year window.

Our metric counts rows per week — i.e. how many package/variety/grade combinations were quoted. If strawberries are quoted in a similar spread of packages every week from April to November, the count looks flat even while actual *volume* swings enormously. So listing density measures **breadth of offering**, not abundance.

So **yes, your skepticism is justified** — but the flaw is narrower than "terminal data is invalid," and it's worth being precise about:

**Terminal data answers "when can you buy California X in San Francisco," not "when is X harvested near San Francisco."** California grows strawberries in Oxnard (winter–spring), Santa Maria (spring–fall) and Salinas-Watsonville (summer). Origin-filtering to "California" unions all three staggered seasons into one ~9-month band. The `district` field would separate them, but it's `N/A` on 52,070 of 53,485 rows.

**Critically, the error is crop-specific.** Cherries came out right — CA cherries are a concentrated San Joaquin/Central Coast crop with one short season, so union-across-districts changes nothing. The distortion is large only for crops grown across many districts with staggered timing (strawberries, blueberries). That's why cherries looked plausible and strawberries didn't.

1. **Foodwise as the primary source.** It *is* Bay Area farmers-market data, curated by the org running those markets — correct scope by construction. Cost: month granularity, so we'd drop the "week-level" claim in the banner.
2. **Keep MARS, add Foodwise as a validation oracle.** Derive week-level spans as now, then automatically compare each crop against Foodwise's months and flag ones where MARS is substantially broader. Keeps precision; catches exactly the strawberry failure mode.
3. **Shipping-point data** (harvest-side, what we used originally for cherries) — accurate for harvest timing, but only ~12 fruits and 2 vegetables. Not enough for a poster.

steps.text:
Let me propose a structure before moving files, since this is a big rename.

**The flow has three stages, and the current layout hides all three:** `scripts/mars/` mixes fetching with deriving, `scripts/lib/` and `scripts/regions/build.ts` both render, and `raw/` sits under `src/data/` while only build-time code touches it.

Proposed — one top-level `data/` holding the whole pipeline, so `src/` stays purely the app:

```
data/
  README.md          ← the flow, in one screen
  regions/           WHAT each poster shows: crop lists (source of truth)
    index.ts  sfbay.ts  ny.ts
  fetch/             ① writes raw/       · network · needs MARS_API_KEY
    run.ts  mars.ts
  raw/               ② committed API responses · never hand-edited
    mars/ca/*.jsonc
  build/             ③ reads raw/ → writes __generated__/ · no network
    run.ts  season.ts  produce.ts  render.ts
  __generated__/     ④ output · the app imports this
    sfbay.ts  ny.ts
  columnar.ts        format of raw/      (shared by ① and ③)
  types.ts           schema of __generated__ (shared by ③ and the app)
  index.ts           regions list the app imports
```

The two shared contracts sit at the root deliberately: `columnar.ts` defines what `raw/` *is*, `types.ts` defines what `__generated__` *is* — one per artifact.

**And the commands split to match the directories**, which is the clearest expression of your fetch-vs-derive distinction:

```bash
bun run fetch            # → raw/          (network, resumable, --limit, --force)
bun run regions          # raw/ → __generated__/   (offline, what CI verifies)
```

Today one command does both via `--pull`, which is exactly the conflation you're pointing at.

**Left alone:** `scripts/build.ts` stays as the app bundler — top level becomes `src/` (app), `data/` (pipeline), `scripts/` (project tooling). And `src/lib/season.ts` stays put; `peakMidpoint` is genuinely shared by the poster and the build's sort order.

**Cost:** every import path in the pipeline changes, plus `@/src/data/regions` → `@/data` in the app. Mechanical, and CI plus the byte-comparison test will catch anything I get wrong.

Two things worth your call before I start:

1. **`data/` at repo root vs `src/data/`.** I've proposed root, so `src/` means "ships to the browser" — but only `__generated__` and `types.ts` are actually imported by the app, so it's arguable either way.
2. **Splitting `fetch` from `regions`** — good separation, but it's two commands to remember instead of `--pull`.

Want me to proceed as proposed, or adjust either of those?

steps.text:
That's a clearer principle: **each namespace owns its artifacts, its schema, and the code that produces them** — so the code/data split happens *inside* a namespace, not between confusingly-similar siblings.

```
data/
  raw/                        ── everything about raw source data ──
    format.ts                 the columnar .jsonc codec — what these artifacts *are*
    fetch.ts                  CLI ▸ bun run fetch          (network, writes below)
    mars/
      client.ts               MARS API client
      reports.ts              which report carries which commodity
      ca/                     ▸ the artifacts
        cherries.jsonc  peaches.jsonc  …

  regions/                    ── everything about region modules ──
    schema.ts                 zod schema — what __generated__ *is*
    build.ts                  CLI ▸ bun run regions        (offline, writes below)
    render.ts                 produce[] → module text
    sources/
      mars.ts                 raw/mars cache → spans + citation
    sfbay.ts                  crop list: what the sfbay poster shows
    ny.ts                     crop list
    index.ts                  app-facing regions list
    __generated__/            ▸ the artifacts
      sfbay.ts  ny.ts
```

Two things this buys beyond your asks:

- **`sfbay.ts` appears twice by design** — once as the crop list, once under `__generated__/`. The input/output correspondence is visible in the filename.
- **`season.ts` + `produce.ts` collapse into `sources/mars.ts`** (both are "MARS cache → produce entry"), and the `sources/` directory is where a future `foodwise.ts` slots in — making the multi-source future obvious rather than implied.

Naming changes: `columnar.ts` → `raw/format.ts`, `types.ts` → `regions/schema.ts`, both now sitting beside what they describe.

Import shape becomes readable at a glance:
```ts
import { parseCache } from '@/data/raw/format';
import { RegionSchema } from '@/data/regions/schema';
```

steps.text: Let me pull up the visualization guidance before proposing a form change, then diagnose precisely.

The guidance is unambiguous on this: **7–8 series is the ceiling for a stacked/categorical form; past that, facet into small multiples.** We have 15. Our labels save us from the *color* failure (identity isn't color-alone), but the wiggle is exactly the stacked-form failure mode.

Let me confirm the mechanism in our code:

Measured, and it's worse than it looks: **middle ribbons travel 230–266 units on a 600-unit chart** — over 40% of the poster height — purely from what's stacked above them.

**This is structural, not tunable.** In a stacked layout every ribbon's position is the cumulative sum of everything above it, so Tomatoes swings 266 units even though *its own* season is perfectly stable. Cherries is the loudest instigator because it's a tall narrow spike, but every crop contributes. Our slack-distribution makes it worse: the inter-ribbon gaps also breathe week to week, so ribbons wiggle even where nothing above them changed.

Notice the signature in the numbers — travel is smallest at the top and bottom (Cherries 30, Persimmons 30) and largest in the middle (Tomatoes 266). That's the tell-tale accumulation curve, not a data problem.

**The fix that preserves available-vs-peak: give each crop a fixed lane.**

```
now:   ribbon y = Σ(weights above)     → every crop displaces every crop below
lanes: ribbon y = laneTop + laneH/2    → fixed; thickness alone carries the level
       thickness = (weight / 100) × laneH × fill
```

Peak stays a fat band, available a thin one (the 100 : 25 ratio becomes thickness within the lane instead of displacement of neighbours). You keep the `curveBasis` organic edges, the produce colors, the spring→autumn diagonal, and the direct labels — and the travel goes to **zero for all 15 crops**. It also fixes label collisions for free, since a label's vertical position stops moving.

This is what the guidance calls faceting into small multiples, and it's how Foodwise's own chart works — one row per crop.

Alternatives, honestly ranked:

| | effect |
|---|---|
| **Fixed lanes** | removes all travel; keeps peak/available as thickness — **recommended** |
| Soften 100:25 → 100:60 | maybe 40% less travel, but weakens the peak signal, which is the poster's whole point |
| Reorder crops | marginal; already sorted by peak midpoint, which is near-optimal |
| Centered/ThemeRiver | redistributes wiggle, doesn't remove it |

The real cost of lanes: it stops being a *streamgraph*. The ribbons no longer nest into one continuous mass — it reads as a ridgeline of separate bands. That's a genuine aesthetic loss, and it's your call whether the legibility is worth it.

Want me to prototype it so you can compare side by side? It's contained — `buildStreamgraph` is the only function that changes, and I can render both versions at the same size.

steps.text:
Good instinct to push back — fixed lanes would leave the poster ~70% empty, since each crop is in season maybe 15–25 of 52 weeks.

There's a middle ground I should have raised: **lane packing**. Crops whose seasons don't overlap can *share* a lane — Cherries (May–Jun) and Persimmons (Oct–Dec) never coexist, so they can sit in the same row without touching. Zero wiggle, but a fraction of the empty space. Let me compute what it'd actually give us:

exchanges.prompt: Mmm, but there's not a really a rhyme or reason on finding the crop. Maybe I'm okay with that? But there's no objective standard on how to jigsaw all of the crops together. And I don't think it works always in a programmatic case; you're injecting judgement into the diagram now.

steps.text:
You're right, and that's a decisive objection — I should drop it. Packing puts Cherries and Persimmons in one row for no reason other than tile efficiency, the result depends on the greedy order, and it makes the vertical axis mean nothing. That's exactly "injecting judgment into the diagram."

There's a better middle ground I skipped: **a ridgeline (joyplot) — fixed baselines that deliberately overlap.**

```
lanes (sparse)          ridgeline (overlapping)
 ────╱▔╲──────           ────╱▔╲──────
                    →        ╱▔╲   ← rows spaced closer than the ribbons are tall,
 ──────╱▔╲────          ──────╱▔╲──   so fat parts overlap and lean parts don't
```

Each crop keeps its **own fixed baseline** — `y = i × spacing`, never moving — but `spacing` is set *smaller* than a peak ribbon's height. Where a crop is at peak it rises into its neighbour's band; where it's out of season it's flat and the neighbour shows through. Drawn back-to-front, the overlaps read as depth rather than collision.

That gets all four things at once:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Density** | overlap reclaims exactly the space lanes waste — tune `spacing` to trade density against clarity |
| **Wiggle** | zero. A baseline is `i × spacing`; nothing above it can move it |
| **Meaning** | row = one crop, ordered by peak midpoint. The vertical axis keeps the seasonal diagonal |
| **peak vs available** | still height — a fat ridge vs a low swell |

It also suits what we already draw: the fill-plus-same-colour-stroke marks give each ridge a clean edge against the one behind, which is what makes joyplots readable rather than muddy.

The honest trade: it's no longer one continuous mass, and where several crops peak together (July–August) the overlap will be busiest — that's precisely where a stacked chart is *also* worst, but here it degrades into layering rather than displacement.

**The lower-effort alternative**, if you'd rather not change form at all: our baseline is naive — we anchor the top and redistribute slack into the gaps, which actively amplifies movement. The literature fix (Byron & Wattenberg's wiggle-minimising baseline, `d3.stackOffsetWiggle`) chooses the baseline that minimises total slope. Same streamgraph, same density, meaningfully less travel — but *some* travel always remains, because it's inherent to stacking.

I'd try the ridgeline. Want me to prototype it against the current version at the same size so you can judge the density trade directly?

exchanges.prompt: Oh, interesting, how does d3.stackOffsetWiggle work? Does it choose the ordering of the crops, then?

steps.text: Good question — and they're **orthogonal**, which matters for us. Let me check the actual implementation rather than describe it from memory:

**No — offset and order are completely separate concerns in d3.** `stackOffsetWiggle(series, order)` takes the order as a *given* parameter and only chooses the baseline.

**How the offset works.** Walking week by week, for each layer it computes how far that layer's *midpoint* would move since the previous week:

```js
s3 = (own thickness change) / 2        // its midpoint rises by half its own growth
   + Σ (thickness changes below it)    // everything underneath shoves it bodily
```

Then it shifts the whole baseline by the **thickness-weighted average** of those movements, in the opposite direction (`y -= s2 / s1`, where `s1` is total thickness). So it can't stop layers moving *relative to each other* — that's fixed by the data — but it cancels the average motion, weighting fat layers most. Which is the right priority: a fat ribbon wiggling is visually loud, a hairline wiggling isn't.

**Ordering is a separate family**, and `stackOrderInsideOut` is the one Byron & Wattenberg pair with it: sort by when each series peaks, then deal them alternately onto a top and bottom pile so the biggest end up in the middle and the small ones on the outside — because outer layers move least.

**Two things that matter for us specifically:**

1. **`insideOut` would destroy our diagonal.** Our peak-midpoint sort is essentially d3's `appearance` order, which produces the spring→autumn reading. `insideOut` takes that order and *interleaves* it top/bottom, so Cherries and Persimmons would end up adjacent at one edge. Minimum wiggle and a meaningful vertical axis are in genuine tension — we'd be trading the poster's clearest idea for smoothness.

2. **It assumes a contiguous stack, and ours isn't.** d3's layers touch. We insert `ROW_GAP` *plus redistributed slack* between ribbons — and that gap-breathing is a wiggle source d3 doesn't model at all. Adopting the wiggle offset means dropping the slack redistribution and letting ribbons touch, which turns the poster into one solid mass of colour bands. That's a real aesthetic change — though notably in the direction you wanted, since the white gaps are a big part of the current whitespace.

So the honest framing is three positions, not two:

| | wiggle | density | vertical axis means |
|---|---|---|---|
| **True streamgraph** (wiggle offset, contiguous, `appearance` order) | much reduced, not zero | highest — no gaps | season order ✓ |
| same + `insideOut` order | lowest | highest | nothing ✗ |
| **Ridgeline** (fixed baselines, overlapping) | zero | tunable via spacing | season order ✓ |

Given you want density *and* a meaningful order, the first row is a smaller change than I implied earlier — keep our existing sort, drop the slack-gap redistribution, use the wiggle baseline. I could prototype that alongside the ridgeline; they're different enough that seeing both at poster size is worth more than more argument.

exchanges.prompt: Okay, let's try out this d3.stackOffsetWiggle thing. I don't 100% understand how we handle the scenario where January truly has nothing yet, but I want to see what this is.

steps.text: Let me implement it. Note your January question has a concrete answer in the algorithm: when every layer is zero, total thickness `s1 = 0`, so `if (s1)` skips the baseline adjustment entirely — the stack just holds still, and all 15 zero-height ribbons collapse onto one line.
That's a true streamgraph now — but it has traded one problem for a worse one. Let me try the centering offset, which is a one-word change:

Both are worth seeing, and I'd call the experiment informative but unsuccessful. Honest read:

**Wiggle** — the whole mass migrates diagonally top-left → bottom-right, leaving two large empty triangles. Net whitespace is *worse* than what we started with.

**Silhouette** — better, since centering removes most of the drift, but the mass still wanders down-right, and now there are deep V-notches cutting through the whole stack.

**The root cause is a mismatch between the form and the data.** Streamgraphs assume *many concurrent series with smoothly varying magnitudes* — that's what makes a thick, continuous river. Ours is the opposite:

- **Seasons are sequential, not concurrent.** At any given week only 3–5 of 15 crops are non-zero, so the stack is inherently thin and has to wander to stay centered. That wandering *is* the whitespace.
- **Magnitude is nearly binary** (25 or 100). Every peak/available boundary is a 4× step, so the silhouette scallops instead of flowing. Those notches are the same weight cliff that made the double humps.

So the original hypothesis — streamgraph means less whitespace — doesn't hold for disjoint seasons. The form can't create density that the data doesn't have; it can only redistribute the emptiness, and it does so by moving crops around, which is exactly the wiggle we were trying to kill.

**Which points back at the ridgeline**, for a reason I underweighted earlier: with fixed rows, the empty space *means something* — "not in season" — instead of being an artifact of the mass drifting. January is genuinely bare either way; the question is only whether the emptiness reads as information or as a hole. And a ridgeline's overlap reclaims exactly the vertical space that plain lanes waste.

Three ways to go:

1. **Ridgeline** — fixed baselines, overlapping. Zero wiggle, meaningful emptiness, tunable density. My recommendation.
2. **Revert** to the anchored stack we had, accepting the wiggle.
3. **Keep silhouette** — genuinely the prettiest of the three as an object, if you're willing to trade legibility for it.

The code currently sits on silhouette; switching among these is a small change in one function. Want me to build the ridgeline so you can compare all four?

steps.text: Let me build it so you can judge it directly:

Clearly the best of the four — you can trace any single crop, the spring→autumn diagonal is unmistakable, and the mesa shape (flat top = peak, shoulders = available) reads well. But `RIDGE_OVERLAP = 2.4` is too aggressive: front ridges are burying the ones behind, and only about half the labels survive. Let me dial it back:
That's a decisive improvement. At `RIDGE_OVERLAP = 1.5`, **all 15 crops are traceable and 14 labels render cleanly** — versus roughly half at 2.4.

| `stackOffsetWiggle` | mass drifts diagonally; *more* whitespace, in two corners |
| `stackOffsetSilhouette` | centred, but still drifts and scallops badly |
| **ridgeline @ 1.5** | zero travel, all 15 crops traceable, 14 labels clean |

**Why the streamgraph couldn't win here:** it assumes many *concurrent* series with smoothly varying magnitude. Ours are sequential and nearly binary — only 3–5 of 15 crops are non-zero in any week, and every peak/available boundary is a 4× step. So the stack is inherently thin, has to wander to stay balanced, and scallops at every transition. The form can't manufacture density the data doesn't have; it can only move the emptiness around.

The ridgeline instead makes the emptiness *mean* something: a flat baseline says "not in season yet." And `RIDGE_OVERLAP` is now a single knob trading density against occlusion — 1.5 is a good default, but it's one constant if you want to push either way.

steps.text: Your last point is the important one — if the peak *timeshifts* between years, summing volume across seasons smears it, and the "valleys" may be nothing but misaligned peaks. Let me check whether that's what's happening:

The data confirms your hypothesis exactly. Every artifact is a misalignment ghost:

```
peaches     2022  peak wk 21-31
            2023  peak wk 24-34      ← each year is ONE clean peak…
            2024  peak wk 29-35
            SUM   23,24,25, 27,…35   ← …but 8 weeks apart, so the sum smears
                                        and gaps at 26 where '22 fades and '24 hasn't started

persimmons  2022  46-49    2023  45-49    2024  44-47
            SUM   44,45,46, ✗47, 48,49    ← hole at 47 is pure artifact

tomatoes    2022  26-41    2023  29 only  2024  26-42
            SUM   29                      ← the vanishing spike
```

**So the order of operations is wrong.** We sum three seasons and *then* threshold. Since the seasons don't align, the sum has ridges where years coincide and troughs where they don't — and the troughs are the "short valleys" you spotted. Tomatoes collapses to one week for the same reason: only week 29 happens to clear 75% of a *summed* max that three noisy years jointly inflated.

**The fix follows from your own framing: stop pretending there's a definitive range, and report consensus instead.**

Classify each season *on its own terms* (its own max), then vote across seasons:

```
per season:  peak = ≥75% of THAT season's max, available = ≥25%
across:      peak      = peak in a majority of seasons
             available = in season in a majority of seasons
```

Worked against the real data, this fixes all four cases and produces contiguous bands:

| crop | now | with voting |
|---|---|---|
| peaches | 23–35 with a hole at 26 | **24–34** |
| persimmons | 44–46, 48–49 | **45–49** |
| blackberries | 26–27, 31–37 | **30–36** |
| tomatoes | week 29 only | **26–41** |

And it gives the bands a much better meaning than they currently have:

- **peak** = "most years, this is at its best"
- **available** = "some years yes, some no" — precisely the timeshift uncertainty, rendered as the shoulders

That's honest about the thing you identified as unattainable, rather than papering over it. It also preserves a genuine double harvest: if a crop really does peak twice *every* year, both windows win their votes and both survive — while a one-off valley gets outvoted.

One guard needed: a season with almost no data shouldn't get a full vote. Blackberries has a stray 2025 row that would be "peak" for 2025 on its own, since it's that season's only data point. I'd require a season to have some minimum coverage before it votes.

Want me to implement it? It replaces `weeklyVolume` + `spansFromVolume` with a per-season classify-then-vote, and I can show the before/after ridgeline.

Now the voting derivation:

**Blueberries — no consensus at all.** The three seasons peak at weeks 20–22, 24 & 26, and 23. They *never overlap*, so no week wins a majority and the crop lost its peak entirely (which is also why it sorted to the bottom — `peakMidpoint` returns Infinity).

Let me rewrite the tests for the new derivation:

That's a decisive improvement — clean mesas, all labels legible, and the scalloping is gone.

**What changed:**

1. **Classify per season, then vote** — the ordering fix. Each season is thresholded against *its own* best week (≥75% peak, ≥25% in season), then a week is peak if a majority of seasons agree. Pooling volume first and thresholding after was creating every artifact you spotted.
2. **Bucket by `report_begin_date`** — the stray 2025 blackberry rows were real shipments from Dec 31, reported Jan 2. No crop-list change needed.

Your framing drove the semantics, and I think they're now defensible to a reader:

> **peak** = most years, this is at its best · **available** = some years yes, some no

The shoulders now literally encode the timeshift uncertainty rather than hiding it — and a crop whose seasons scatter (Blueberries) honestly gets a *wider* peak band than one that's reliable (Cherries).

- **Tomatoes keeps two peaks** (weeks 25–28 and 40, eleven weeks apart) — genuinely far apart, plausibly Imperial Valley early and Central Valley late. It also sorts oddly, because `peakMidpoint` picks the *widest* peak span and ignores the second.

exchanges.prompt: Mmm, we can switch to first peakMidpoint instead of widest.

steps.text: That's a more meaningful metric anyway — "when does it first come into peak" is closer to what the diagonal is telling you than "which of its peaks is longest."

The change is in and CI is green, but I should be straight with you: **the ordering is identical.** It doesn't fix the Tomatoes placement.

The reason is that Tomatoes' peaks are weeks **25–28** (4 weeks) and **40** (1 week) — so its *first* peak is also its *widest*. Both metrics give midpoint 26.5 either way, which sorts it 4th, ahead of Strawberries at 27.

What looks wrong is that its ribbon then stretches to week 42 with a second spike far to the right, so a spring-position row visibly reaches into autumn. **That's the double peak showing, not a sorting bug.** Any single-number ordering will have this property for a two-harvest crop.

The change is still worth keeping on its merits — "when does it arrive at its best" is a better rule than "which peak ran longest", and it'll matter as soon as a crop's later peak is its longer one (a genuine spring-and-autumn harvest would currently be filed under autumn).

- **Accept it** — it's true, and arguably the most interesting row on the poster

exchanges.prompt: What does "the voting" mean?

steps.text:
Fair — I've been leaning on the term. Concretely, "the voting" is the derivation I put in place two steps ago, replacing "pool all years then threshold."

**Per season, independently:**
```
find that season's biggest week
  ≥75% of it  → peak
  ≥25% of it  → available
  below       → not in season
```

**Then across seasons, week by week:** count how many seasons called week *N* peak, and how many called it in-season. A majority (2 of 3) wins.

So each season casts one vote per week, and the week's label is whatever most seasons said. That's what fixed the peaches smear — the years are compared *as shapes* rather than summed into one curve.

The subtlety relevant to tomatoes: because each season is measured against **its own** max, a quiet season's late bump can clear 75% *of that season* even though it's small in absolute pounds. So "peak at week 40" means at least two seasons independently had a week-40 bump that was large **relative to their own best week** — which the pooled view hides, since pooling is dominated by whichever season shipped most.

That's exactly why the pooled profile shows one clean peak at ~29 while the vote shows two. Let me show you which seasons are voting for week 40:

Now I can see where it comes from:

| season | shape | week 40 |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | spiky — peak weeks 26, 29, 37, **41** | 65% of own best |
| 2023 | one clean peak at 29 | 38% |
| 2024 | peak 26–31 **and 40–42** | 80% |

So 2022 and 2024 both vote for a late bump; 2023 doesn't. Two of three is a majority, hence the second peak.

And on your varietal hypothesis — **not supported for this commodity**, but you're right about the general principle. Let me verify against an outside source:

steps.text:
**The double peak is real, and verified.** [UC ANR's fresh-market tomato production guide](https://ucanr.edu/sites/default/files/2018-11/294660.pdf) and the [CA crop profile](https://ipmdata.ipmcenters.org/documents/cropprofiles/CAtomatoes-freshmarket.pdf) describe exactly this: Central Valley fields are planted March–July for harvest June–October, with a **distinct fall crop planted in June/July**. Spring planting → summer harvest; fall planting → October harvest. Our two peaks (weeks 26–31 and 40–42) match that pattern, and 2023 missing the second one is a real year-to-year difference, not noise.

**On varietals — you're right in principle, wrong for this row.** `Tomatoes` has `variety: null` on every row, so nothing is smushed *within* it. But MARS does the varietal split one level up: `Tomatoes, Plum Type` is its own commodity in the same report, as are Cherry and Grape Type in the terminal data. So **Roma is addable as its own crop row today** — it just isn't hiding inside "Tomatoes" (which means round/slicing). Heirloom doesn't exist in MARS at all; it's a wholesale grading system, and heirlooms are a farmers-market category.

## Encoding uncertainty

We already compute the raw material and then throw it away: **the vote counts**. Week 40 is "2 of 3 seasons", week 29 is "3 of 3" — and right now both render identically.

**Data.** I'd add one optional field to each span:

```ts
{ level: 'peak', from: 26, to: 31, confidence: 1 }     // every season agreed
{ level: 'peak', from: 40, to: 42, confidence: 0.67 }  // two of three
```

Optional matters: hand-authored entries (Strawberries, NY Blueberries) have no vote data, and absent should mean "not measured" rather than a fake 1.0.

**Visual.** Three options, roughly increasing in ambition:

1. **Opacity ∝ confidence** — literally what you suggested. A 3/3 peak is solid; a 2/3 peak sits around 70% opaque. Cheap, and it reads immediately as "this one's less reliable." Risk: with overlapping ridges, translucency lets the ribbon behind show through, which could muddy rather than inform.
2. **Soft edges** — fade the ribbon across the weeks where seasons disagree about the start/end, using an SVG gradient. This targets *timing* variance specifically, which is the thing you identified as unattainable. More faithful, more work.
3. **Ghost ribbons** — draw each season's own ribbon at 1/n opacity, overlapping. Where seasons agree the alpha accumulates to solid; where they disagree it's faint. This is the most literal possible rendering of the vote — the picture *is* the data — but it needs per-season spans in the generated file, which is a much bigger data change.

**My recommendation: (1) now, (2) later if it's not enough.** Opacity is a small, reversible change to schema + derivation + one render line, and it'll tell us quickly whether the variance is even visually interesting across these 15 crops — Cherries and Blueberries differ a lot in agreement, so we'd see it immediately. (3) is the most beautiful idea but I'd want to know the encoding earns its keep before restructuring the data for it.

Worth noting one honest caveat before we build any of it: with only **three seasons**, confidence takes just four values (0, ⅓, ⅔, 1). That's a coarse signal — enough to distinguish "all years agree" from "one outlier", but not a smooth gradient. Pulling more years would sharpen it, and the reports go back further than 2022.

Want me to implement (1), or pull more seasons first so the measure has more resolution?

steps.text:
Yes — and with a chosen font you probably *should* calculate, for a reason that isn't the obvious one.

The obvious argument is determinism, and it's real but secondary. The actual reason is that **picking a webfont makes runtime measurement worse, not better.** Right now the font stack is `system-ui` — already present, zero load time, so measuring during render always measures the real thing. The moment you self-host a WOFF2, there's a window where the font hasn't loaded and the browser is painting a fallback. Measure during that window and you get the fallback's advances baked into the chip geometry, and they stay wrong unless you explicitly await `document.fonts.ready` and re-render. So a webfont would force you to add a load-gate and a second render pass just to keep measurement honest — whereas precomputed metrics sidestep the race entirely.

Precomputing also fixes the hydration shift I flagged, since the server and browser would agree.

Two caveats worth knowing before you commit:

- **Kerning.** Summing per-character advances ignores kern pairs, which browsers apply by default. It's a sub-percent error on names like these, and `CHIP_PAD_X` swallows it — but it means "calculated" is very slightly approximate, not exact.
- **Load failure.** If the webfont fails, the fallback renders at different widths and the chips are wrong. `font-display` and `size-adjust` on the `@font-face` are the usual mitigations.

If you do go that way, it fits an idiom this repo already has: extract the advance table from the font file into a generated module, same shape as `data/regions/__generated__` with a test asserting it regenerates byte-identically. Then a font swap is "rerun the generator," and CI catches a stale table — which is the property you were asking for originally, just enforced instead of remembered.

Until you pick one, I'd leave `textWidth()` as it is. It's the right call specifically *because* the stack is `system-ui`, and it's about fifteen lines to swap out later.

steps.text:
Researched. Answering the licensing question first, then the poles.

## Licensing

Your premise holds: everything on Google Fonts is open source and free for commercial use, under one of three licenses — the SIL Open Font License (most of the library), Apache 2.0, or the Ubuntu Font License. One catch that matters for you specifically: **if you distribute the font files you must ship the license text with them**, and self-hosting a WOFF2 on GitHub Pages counts as distributing. That's an argument for finally building the `/about/licenses` page already on your list. The OFL's Reserved Font Name clause also means a modified font can't keep its original name — relevant only if you end up subsetting aggressively enough to re-generate the family.

## What actually constrains the choice

Worth naming before the fun part: this poster is ~40 small text objects (15 crop labels at 12 units, 24 month labels at 11) and **one** display moment, the title at 30. So character is affordable in exactly one place, and legibility-at-small-print governs everywhere else. That points at a pair rather than a single face — which is convenient, because it means the "extreme opinions" exercise is really about the title.

## Four poles

**1. 1970s natural-foods co-op — [Fraunces](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Fraunces)**
Undercase Type's revival of the Windsor / Souvenir / Cooper lineage — the exact register of health-food packaging, Whole Earth Catalog, and every co-op sign from that era. The strongest candidate for your purpose because it's a *variable* font with `SOFT` (ink wetness) and `WONK` (the lean on `h`/`n`/`m`, flagged terminals) axes. You can literally dial how much opinion you want rather than picking a fixed amount, and its `opsz` axis means it could plausibly serve the small labels too.

**2. 19th-century woodtype crate label — [Alfa Slab One](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Alfa+Slab+One), [Ultra](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Ultra), [Bevan](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Bevan)**
Heavy Egyptian slabs. Alfa Slab One descends from a Thorowgood foundry Egyptian, Bevan reworks a 1930s Heinrich Jost slab, Ultra nods to Clarendon. This is the agricultural-fair-poster, fruit-crate-label pole: loud, sturdy, unmistakably American vernacular. Display only — none of these will survive at 12 units.

**3. Hand-lettered chalkboard — [Caveat](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Caveat), [Amatic SC](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Amatic+SC)**
The literal market-stall sign. I'd push back on this one, and not on taste grounds: [Ohio State's agricultural extension guidance on farm-market signage](https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/anr-70) recommends clean sans-serifs, one font per sign, and says printed signs beat handwritten ones when the lettering isn't consistently legible. The people who advise actual market vendors are steering away from the aesthetic that *represents* markets in stock imagery. There's a real irony here worth respecting: your poster is a reference document people scan for a specific crop, not a booth sign read at twenty feet.

**4. The anti-pole — [Inter](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Inter), [Archivo](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Archivo)**
Neutral grotesque, zero farm character, maximum data legibility. Worth naming because it's roughly where you already are: `system-ui` resolves to SF Pro / Segoe / Roboto, all in this family. Choosing nothing *is* choosing this pole.

## What I'd blend

Fraunces for the title at high `WONK`/`SOFT`, paired with a warm humanist sans for labels and axis — [Work Sans](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Work+Sans) or [Karla](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Karla) rather than Inter, since a little warmth in the workhorse keeps the pairing from reading as two unrelated decisions. That gets you the farm register where it's readable and legibility where it's needed.

The genuinely interesting variant: **Fraunces for everything**, using `opsz` to drop the wonk at small sizes automatically. Riskier in print, but it's the option that would make the poster look designed rather than assembled — and it's only possible because the axes exist.

Two practical consequences: a four-axis variable font is heavy, so you'd want to subset to Latin (you've been counting KB carefully elsewhere), and picking any webfont is the trigger to switch `textWidth()` from runtime measurement to precomputed metrics, for the FOUT reason from before.

Sources: [Google Fonts FAQ](https://developers.google.com/fonts/faq) · [Google Design on Fraunces](https://design.google/library/a-new-take-on-old-style-typeface) · [Undercase Type](https://undercase.xyz/fonts/fraunces) · [OSU Extension ANR-70](https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/anr-70)

## My opinion

**Excellent title face, wrong label face — and a different vibe than the one you said you wanted.**

It's more legible at 14 units than I expected (the pencil rendering thickened what would otherwise be Didone hairlines). But look at what the roughness *communicates* at each size. In the title it reads as deliberate — hand-drawn, characterful. In the labels it reads as a **printing defect**: not "someone wrote this," which is what Caveat gave you, but "this scanned badly." That's the distinction that matters for a poster people consult rather than glance at.

The tonal point is the bigger one. Fredericka's skeleton is Modern No. 20 — a 19th-century Didone — just drawn by hand. So it lands as Victorian apothecary / circus bill / antique print. Caveat's skeleton is actual handwriting, which lands as chalkboard and market stall. You said Caveat's vibe was what you were going for; Fredericka is a genuinely nice thing, but it isn't that thing.

Three hard constraints on top of taste:

- **Single weight, 400 only.** You lose bold entirely. That matters because small text on a busy poster is exactly where you want the extra weight — I had to drop `LABEL_WEIGHT` from 600 to 400 to test it fairly. It also creates a subtle hazard: ask for 600 anyway and the browser fakes it, and canvas `measureText` and SVG rendering don't necessarily agree on synthetic-bold widths, which would quietly desync the chips from their text.
- **203 KB vs 74 KB**, 2.7×. Non-blocking, per above, but still a lot to ship.
- Its own specimen guidance says it's not for body copy.

**What I'd do:** Fredericka for the title, something quiet for the labels. That's the standard display-plus-text pairing and it puts Fredericka exactly where it's strong. I'd avoid Fredericka title + Caveat labels, though — two hand-drawn voices at once is noise, not personality. Fredericka title with a warm sans for labels, or Caveat throughout as you had it.

steps.text:
Your instinct on the alternative is right, and I'd push the reasoning further: the available height is a *claim about the data* — how strongly the crop is in season — so retuning it to buy layout headroom would make the drawing lie to fix a spacing problem.

Better: the overlap has a derivable ceiling. Row *i*'s available band sits `0.25 × ridgeHeight` above its baseline, and row *i+1*'s peak reaches `(RIDGE_OVERLAP − 1) × spacing` above that same baseline. Setting those equal gives a hard limit of `1 / (1 − 0.25)` = 1.333 — and 1.5 is past it, which is exactly why Raspberries buries Tomatoes.

steps.name: Bash
steps.detail: cd /Users/germanium/code/vertumnus; bun run format >/dev/null 2>&1; bun run ci 2>&1|tail -5; SP=/pri

steps.text:
Fixed, and Tomatoes gained more than the shoulder — its **gap between the two harvests** is now visible as a dip to the available line, where Raspberries previously filled it in. The double-harvest reading we verified against UC ANR is legible on the poster for the first time.

`RIDGE_OVERLAP` is now derived rather than picked:

```ts
const AVAILABLE_SHARE = LEVEL_BAND[Level.Available].lower / PEAK_HEIGHT;  // 0.25
const RIDGE_OVERLAP = (1 / (1 - AVAILABLE_SHARE)) * 0.9;                  // 1.2
```

Ceiling is 1.333; 1.5 was 12% past it, which is why the collision existed. The `0.9` leaves 0.1 spacings of visible clearance so the available band reads as a band rather than a hairline — sitting exactly on the limit would make the two edges coincide.

Two things fall out of doing it this way rather than typing `1.2`:

- The constraint is now **self-maintaining**. If you ever do revisit the available level, the overlap follows and the collision can't silently return.
- The label invariant survives untouched. `LABEL_RISE` is `RIDGE_OVERLAP / 2`, so labels always sit at exactly 50% of ridge height *regardless* of the overlap value — meaning available (25%) can never reach a label and peak (100%) always does. That's why no label placement changed despite the geometry moving.

Ridges are shorter now, since the rows still span the same height with less overlap between them. To my eye it reads calmer and the individual seasons are easier to separate, but it is a real trade against the density the overlap was there to buy — if you want it back, raising the `0.9` toward `1.0` recovers height right up to the collision point.

```
manual (paper, Fig. 5)     ·················-----###########-------············  peak 23–33
all CA · 6yr               ···········----#############------------------······  peak 16–28
all CA · 3yr (22-24)       ··········-----++###########------------------······  peak 18–28
Salinas-Watsonville · 6yr  ················----+###############------··········  peak 22–36
Salinas-Watsonville · 3yr  ················----+#############++------··········  peak 22–34
```

**Whole-state MARS is off by seven weeks** — peak 16–28 against the paper's 23–33, and in season 12–46 (35 weeks) against 18–40 (23). The `why:` note on the manual entry is exactly right about the cause, and the district curves quantify it:

| district | best week | volume |
|---|---|---|
| Salinas-Watsonville | 24 | 4,609M lb |
| Santa Maria | 20 | 3,852M lb |
| Oxnard | 16 | 1,963M lb |
| Orange–San Diego | 14 | 44M lb |

The southern districts together out-ship Salinas-Watsonville, so the aggregate peak gets dragged early.

**Filter to Salinas-Watsonville and MARS reproduces the paper.** Six years gives 22–36 against 23–33 — start within a week, tail three weeks longer, which is expected since the paper is a three-year average and ours spans six including the drift. On a matched three-year window it's 22–34 against 23–33, essentially exact.

Three things fall out of this that I'd flag:

1. **The reports docblock is wrong in a way that matters.** It says "shipped volume put the peak at weeks 23–34 against that curve's 23–33" — but whole-state volume gives 18–28 even on the 3-year window. That 23–34 figure only reproduces from the *district-filtered* subset (22–34). Both of your instincts are right to be suspicious, for reasons worth naming:

**The landmark doesn't scale and fights the subject.** You'd need a bespoke illustration per region — you've said 5+ — and what's the landmark for *New York State*? Not the Statue of Liberty; the poster is about the Finger Lakes and Hudson Valley. A bridge says "tourist print of San Francisco," not "what's good this week." It also creates a second focal point competing with the ridgeline.

**The stock photo has harder problems than tacky.** A generic market crowd is identical across regions, which undermines the regional specificity that *is* the product. Plus: photos of identifiable people carry model-release questions if this is ever distributed, screen-res stock prints badly, and a raster photo blows the byte budget you've been careful about.

## What I'd do instead

**Region-specific imagery, yes — but the region's *fruit*, not its landmark.**

The [USDA Pomological Watercolor Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomological_Watercolor_Collection) is 7,497 watercolours of fruit varieties painted 1886–1942, in the US public domain, held by the National Agricultural Library — *the same department that publishes the MARS data the poster is built from*. A Watsonville strawberry for sfbay, an apple for NY. It's on-subject, region-specific, scales (one image per region, from a library of thousands), and the provenance is a genuinely nice fact rather than decoration.

One ornament, not fifteen. A watercolour per crop would fight the ridgeline; a single one at the masthead does the work.

## But I'd do this first, before any imagery

The gap between "technical chart" and "poster" is mostly **typography and composition**, and it costs no assets:

- **A masthead** — region name, a subtitle ("What's in season at the farmers' market"), an edition line. Right now it's one centred string in a green bar.
- **The footer you already have TODO'd** — citations as fine print. Posters have fine print; here it doubles as the honesty the project cares about.
- **Margins instead of a border.** The sage frame currently reads as a certificate. Generous white margin with the colour used sparingly reads as print.

That sequence also protects customizability: masthead and footer are structural, so they survive whatever you do with imagery later.

**Free bonus that scales infinitely:** derive each region's accent colour from its own crop palette rather than hardcoding sage. No assets, no per-region work, and the poster's identity comes from its data.

Masthead before footer because it sets the type scale the footer keys off — and the footer is the bigger job, since it plumbs `item.sources` through to the artifact, which is the first time the citations you've been careful about actually appear on the printed thing.

**One URL, not three.** This is a printed artifact — every URL on it is dead weight unless someone would actually type it. `vertumnus.fyi/about/sources` can carry the repo link, the full per-crop citations, and the method write-up. Putting the GitHub URL on the poster itself would be clutter that serves a reader who's already at a computer.

**The most important line is an honesty line.** The headline claims *farmers' market*, but the data is wholesale shipment volume from named growing districts — a good proxy, not the literal thing. The footer is where that gets stated plainly, and it's also what makes the district filtering legible to someone who didn't build it.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Seasons derived from USDA AMS Market News shipment volumes, 2019–2024.        │
│  Salinas-Watsonville, San Joaquin Valley and Central California districts.     │
│                                                  vertumnus.fyi/about/sources  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   left: provenance, 2 lines                              right: where to go
```

Left carries what the data *is* and when; right carries where to learn more. Both at ~8 units, in the muted green, on the sage below the card.

Two things worth deciding before I build it:

- **Derived or hardcoded?** The generated citations are long (`USDA AMS Market News — Fresno, CA Truck, Air and Boat Movement Report (FR_FV170); California-grown, 2019–2024 seasons, … raw cache: …`) — far too long for fine print. To derive the footer from `region.items[].sources` rather than hardcoding it, sources need a short `credit` field alongside the full `title`. That's the right call for multi-region and for a hand-authored crop with a different source, but it's schema surface and a regeneration.
- **A one-line key?** You dropped the legend as unnecessary, and I agreed. But the footer is fine print, where `Solid: at its best most years · Pale: only some years` costs one line rather than a legend block. Worth it or still noise?

steps.text:
My phrasing was sloppy — sorry. The dedupe is **15 → 1**, not 2 → 1:

```
sfbay: 15 crops → 15 source entries → 1 distinct credit
```

Every crop carries its own source entry, so without deduping the footer would print the same line fifteen times. That's the dedupe you'd expect.

The "both reports" remark was about a *different* question: whether those 15 collapse to **one** line or **two**. The crops split across two AMS offices (Fresno and El Centro), so if the credit string named the report — `…Fresno, CA Truck, Air and Boat Movement Report (FR_FV170)` — the 15 would collapse to two distinct strings and the poster would carry two nearly identical credit lines differing only by an office name that means nothing to a reader. Omitting the report name is what makes them collapse all the way to one. The report code still lives in the crop list and the raw cache, where it's actually useful.

The footer derives from `region.items[].sources` rather than being hardcoded, deduped, so a region drawing on several sources gets a line each and `footerH` grows with them. The card shrinks to make room rather than the footer overlapping it.

Three judgment calls worth surfacing:

- **The district names are on the poster.** That's the honesty line: the headline says *farmers' market*, the data is wholesale shipment volume, and naming Salinas-Watsonville / San Joaquin / Central District is what lets a reader see the scope rather than take the claim on faith.
- **`districtLabel` converts `SALINAS-WATSONVILLE CALIFORNIA` → `Salinas-Watsonville`** — stripping the redundant state and title-casing. Presentation logic in the data layer, but the credit *is* presentation, so it belongs with the string it builds.
- **Fine print is set in the headline's dark green, not the overline's lighter one.** At 8 units the lighter green lands around 4.4:1 on sage, just under AA, and small text needs contrast more than it needs to be quiet — the size already makes it quiet.

Only real omission: no repo link on the poster, per the one-URL reasoning. It belongs on `/about/sources` alongside the method and the full per-crop citations — which is also where the long-form report codes now live, since the credit deliberately drops them.

Remind me again about the licensing for fonts and other libraries; we only need to put that on the /about page, right, and not on the poster itself?

steps.text: Both — the colour change, and let me get concrete about the licences rather than assert:

Footer is now the region colour. I measured it rather than eyeballing: **4.22:1 on the sage**, just under AA's 4.5 for body text. Your call and a defensible one — it's fine print, not body text — and I've recorded the number in the comment so it's a known trade rather than an oversight. The comment had also gone stale claiming the headline colour, which is now fixed.

## Licensing — yes, `/about` only, not the poster

**Fonts (Noto Serif, Playfair Display — SIL OFL 1.1).** The obligation attaches to distributing the *font software*, i.e. the `.woff2` files. Your site serves those, so the licence has to accompany them — which the `OFL-*.txt` files in `src/fonts/` already satisfy, but they should be reachable and acknowledged from `/about/licenses`. The poster itself doesn't distribute font software; it's a document that *uses* the fonts, and rendered glyphs aren't the font. So no notice on the artifact.

One caveat for later: if you add PDF export with embedded subsets, that's closer to distribution. OFL does permit document embedding, but it'd be worth reading the SIL FAQ at that point rather than assuming.

**JS dependencies.** Only the seven runtime ones ship in the bundle and need notices:

| licence | packages |
|---|---|
| MIT | react, react-dom, react-router, zod, motion |
| ISC | d3-shape, lucide-react |

Both require the copyright and permission notice to travel with copies. The ten build-only deps — oxlint, oxfmt, typescript, tailwindcss, the `@types/*` — don't ship their code, so they need nothing. Tailwind is the one judgment call: its own source isn't bundled, but Preflight's CSS is arguably its work in your output. Cheap to list it and skip the question.

**USDA MARS data** carries no obligation at all — US government work, public domain. The footer credit is courtesy and your own "cite everything" rule, not a requirement. Same will apply to the Pomological watercolours.

So `/about/licenses` needs: two font licences, seven dependency notices, and optionally Tailwind. Working tree is 8 files, CI green.

`Poster` is now placement only — it computes `cardY`/`cardW`/`cardH` and renders `<Masthead>`, the card, and `<Footer>`. Two things the split forced, both improvements:

- **`MASTHEAD_H` and `footerHeight(lines)` are the interface.** The layout needs to know how much room each piece takes without knowing why, so each section exports exactly one number. `footerHeight` had to become a function because the footer grows with the credit count — that dependency was previously tangled into the layout body.

The one judgment call: **colours stayed at the top**, renamed `INK`/`INK_MUTED` from `HEADLINE_COLOR`/`REGION_COLOR`. `INK_MUTED` is used by both the masthead's overline and the footer, so pushing it into either would leave the other importing across the divider — and the palette is genuinely a poster-level decision, since the frame, masthead and fine print have to read as one voice. The comment says so, so it doesn't look like leftover.

I've documented the dependency at `CARD_COLOR` rather than fixing it, since threading a colour through `Ribbons`' props is a bigger call than this refactor — but now it's at least stated at both ends rather than being a coincidence.

steps.text: Now that the header and footer exist, the frame's job is up for grabs. Let me test the version I argued for — white paper, colour only where there's content:

Honest read — it's better on paper and slightly worse on screen.

**Gains, one of them concrete:** the footer contrast goes **4.22 → 6.33:1**, so the sub-AA compromise we accepted two commits ago just disappears. The chart colours also read stronger against true white. And on a home printer, a full-bleed sage band is the worst thing on the page — inkjets streak large flat areas and it burns ink for decoration.

**The real loss is screen-only.** The sage was giving the poster an *edge* — making it read as an object rather than as page content. On paper it doesn't need that: the paper is the edge. So the frame was doing work that only matters in the preview, for a product whose deliverable is the print.

**The problem it exposes:** with the sage gone, the empty Jan–April quadrant is now the loudest thing in the composition. Before, the frame gave the eye colour elsewhere to rest on. This is the citrus gap becoming a design problem rather than just a data one — worth knowing before you tune anything else, because filling it changes the balance again.

steps.text: Let me ground the resolution question first — it depends on what paper sizes you offer:

Two things, one structural and one that may save you a whole mechanism.

## Placement: the lower-left is permanently empty

The ridgeline sorts by peak midpoint, so the chart is inherently a **diagonal band** — which means both off-diagonal corners are structurally empty, not accidentally empty:

- **upper-left** = early months, early crops → empty now, but this is exactly where citrus would land if you ever source it (winter peak sorts to the top rows). Art there has a known claimant.
- **lower-left** = early months, *late* crops → Persimmons and Pomegranates will never exist in January. This stays empty no matter what you add.

So the plate goes lower-left. It fills the void that's currently the loudest compositional problem, competes with no data, and is safe from future crops in a way the top-left isn't.

One plate, isolated on white, no frame or vignette — that's how the collection's images actually look, and it's the register you were circling. Roughly Jan–Apr wide and four or five rows tall.

## The resolution split is probably unnecessary

Your instinct is right in general but the numbers are narrower than they feel:

| | poster width in device px |
|---|---|
| retina screen (64rem @ 2×) | 2048 |
| Letter @ 300dpi | 2550 |
| Tabloid @ 300dpi | 3300 |
| A3 @ 300dpi | 3510 |

Print is only **1.25–1.7×** retina, not the 4× the instinct assumes. At ~28% of the width, one image at **~1000px** covers every preset including A3 — call it 80–150 KB as AVIF, comparable to a font file. A print-only variant would buy you very little for a fair amount of machinery.

Watercolour is also the most forgiving possible subject for upscaling: soft washes have none of the hard edges, text, or fine line work that make upscaled raster look bad. Even a custom 24×36 would hold up better than you'd expect.

So I'd say: ship one image, test-print it, and only build the print-CSS path if the print actually disappoints. Deferring is right either way.

## What I need from you

Which fruit for sfbay? The obvious candidates are a Watsonville strawberry, a Blenheim apricot, or a cherry. Want me to search the collection for candidate plates and show you a few?
